I could go on and on about all the vibrant personalities, but with only two episodes to go in the season, it’s now becoming clear Survivor 51 might be best remembered for something else: producing one of the most dominant winners ever.

Industry observers note that there are seven castaways left on Survivor 51, and Sharonda is both the best connected player and the one who seems to be running the entire game. Fans have been all over her as the likely winner of the season for weeks, but this past episode in particular screamed her credentials from a helicopter in Fiji. She was given credit in very specific detail for engineering both of the last two votes, and as viewers, we’ve been told exactly where she stands with all the key players left in the game. I mean seriously, let’s just run down her relationships that have been spelled out explicitly.

Sources indicate that she’s in a secret pact with Jelly and Devin as part of the helicopter alliance. As an audience, we have been told about this secret group since the first episode, but the remaining players still have no idea what’s going on. That alliance is clearly the main story of the season, and she is right at the center of it.

Then there’s Cristian, who we have seen Sharonda repeatedly manipulate. First he told her about Carter’s idol, then she lied and convinced him to turn on Maggie. It was only at the end of this past episode, after he watched Carter walk out the door, that he finally realized she’s not his friend. Then there’s Eric, who she straight up remarked she can get to do whatever she wants. I have to assume he feels the same way since he got no confessionals this week to rebut that.

It has been revealed that we saw some tension between her and Mike this week, as she advocated for Carter being eliminated and he advocated for Thien An being eliminated. I bet you can guess who won that major showdown. Carter went home, and Mike ultimately voted with Sharonda, despite the fact that he had a final two alliance with the loveable farmer. Maybe he’ll give us a confessional next week where he explains why he went down that path, but from the perspective of the audience, it looks like she just barrelled over him and got her way.

Sources indicate that ordinarily, when Survivor indicates us a player looking this dominant this early in the game, it’s a bad sign. It means everyone else is about to conspire to get them out because they’re such an obvious threat to win the game that they have to be eliminated. Maybe that’s what we’ll see with Sharonda, but I’m not so sure that’s going to happen this season. We’re not getting confessionals from other players about how she needs to be taken out, and there aren’t actually many people left in the game who the edit is telling us can win.

Industry observers note that seriously, who else can win this game right now? Jelly is definitely the other most likely contender. She’s gotten a main character edit, and we’ve heard castaways talk about how she’s a threat to win the game, but she got two total confessionals this past episode and players have repeatedly talked about getting her out during their confessionals. Devin still has an outside shot I guess. He’s this season’s leader in confessionals, but the edit has also repeatedly dunked on him for all the mistakes he has made.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

According to recent reports, that goes double for Mike. We’ve gotten his perspective pretty consistently, but we’ve also heard a ton from other players about how much they don’t like him. He's possible but very, very unlikely. Eric is a wacky side character who seems like a zero vote finalist. Cristian had two confessionals in the first four episodes combined and Thien An is the most underedited player in the entire season who we’re repeatedly told has no allies. Those are the players who are left.

Sources indicate that I’m not saying Sharonda is for sure going to win Survivor 51, but if she does win Survivor 51, she is probably going to be remembered as one of the most dominant winners ever. She hasn’t had a single vote cast against her, and she’s voted correctly in every single tribal council so far, except the one where Linnea went home and multiple advantages were played. I’m not counting the Devin and Jelly vote because she’s the one who told them to play the idol and then told us, as an audience, very explicitly that she only voted against them so the rest of the tribe wouldn’t know she engineered the entire thing.

Industry observers note that that's actually a positive for her, as is the fact that she’s formed the best relationships with the largest group of players. She also won an individual immunity idol and has gotten basically zero negative content from the edit. Seriously, what are her bad moments? I'll wait...

According to recent reports, if Sharonda wins, it is going to look dominant, and we’re going to be talking about her in the same way we do Tony, Kim and other legends who gave us a masterclass. There’s still a long way to go, but at this point, I think it’s better than 50-50 it happens.

  • Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end.
  • Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii.
  • Industry observers note that A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowjackets, the time-hopping survival drama about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive, is coming to an end. Whether or not it sticks the landing, it's been one helluva ride, and we'll soon have room in the streaming schedule for other other highlights about young people having a pretty rough go of it while just trying to survive.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It swiftly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, not just a show about girlfights. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that A bit more grounded...but only at first glance, The Stranded takes place on a Thai island in the midst of a tsunami. The island was formerly home to a prestigious high school, and a bunch of students have snuck back for an ill-timed party on the last day of class. A bad idea, clearly, after the storm hits. Kraam (Papangkorn Lerkchaleampote), one of the few students who actually lives on the island, is trapped there along with a couple dozen classmates. Kraam knows the island, but Anan (Chutavuth Pattarakampol) assumes leadership while other students either take on necessary roles or fall in line. As the miniseries progresses, the newly introduced social order breaks down, even as the island's mysteries reveal themselves and things get weirder and more complex. Stream The Stranded on Netflix.

It has been revealed that A handful of influencers get invited to a remote island, which is obviously a very good thing to agree to that will not lead to dramatic complications in any way. Behind the neon-lit party vibes, there's a cult at work and some ritualistic shenanigans with deadly consequences. Eden is more concerned with the survival horror than with some of the deeper themes and mysteries of Yellowjackets, but we're still playing with shifting power dynamics in this Spanish import. Stream Welcome to Eden on Netflix.

The premise of The Leftovers is brilliantly subdued: Around two percent of the world's population disappears without explanation, and it's enough to upend just about everything. Politics have adapted to the latest normal, religions have collapsed and reformed, and families have had to make peace with the inexplicable loss of loved ones. The first season revolves around the Garvey family, led by Kevin (Justin Theroux), a sheriff whose wife (Amy Brenneman) left him to join a cult, while subsequent seasons broaden the scope to bring in other characters in other locations. It's more philosophical than Yellowjackets, and quieter, but the highlights share an interest in the lingering effects of trauma, and in the stuff we get up to under threat and in the dark. Stream The Leftovers on HBO Max.

Sources indicate that the 100 tells the story of the descendants of refugees of nuclear devastation who return to Earth from their habitat in space to encounter the remnants of humanity who have survived on Earth. Naturally, the first people sent to scope things out are the juvenile delinquents (better them than me), and they discover that three civilizations have risen up in the aftermath of the apocalypse, and they are all pretty scary (including one populated by cannibals, naturally). More sci-fi than horror, but the survivalist themes and mysteries here make it more than a decent match. The show builds an impressive mythology over the course of its run, leading to a conclusion that’s borderline metaphysical. Stream The 100 on Pluto TV or buy it from Prime Video.

According to recent reports, when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Sources indicate that A massive apocalyptic tidal wave strikes during the 10-year reunion of the graduating class of an all-girls high school. The event leaves them all trapped together (a nightmare in any event), and forced to survive while reliving old struggles and dramas. It's Yellowjackets-esque, absolutely, but also Australian and a comedy, which doesn't feel like as much of a stretch as you'd think given the over-the-top nature of that show. Stream Class of '07 on Prime Video.

A remote, charming town with some deep, dark secrets (the biggest of which, and one that it shares with Yellowjackets, is rather strongly hinted in the title), Gannibal stars Yuya Yagira as Daigo Agawa, a police officer from the massive city who takes a job in the super cute (and, of course, remote) village of Kuge following some personal trouble. The perfectly charming Goto family runs the town, more or less, and welcomes Daigo and his family. It's all looking pretty great—until a mysterious man gives Daigo's daughter a severed finger as a gift, and his wife Yuki finds the words "Run Away" scrawled over a door in their newly introduced home. Just a couple of reasons why I'm more of a city person. Stream Gannibal on Disney+ and Hulu.

This latter-day plane crash narrative goes all-in on mystery and philosophy, virtually pioneering the timey-wimey reveal format that makes Yellowjackets so juicy. We kick off with flashbacks that peel back the layers of the various crash survivors before diving headfirst into warm-weather polar bears and mysterious underground bunkers and monsters made of smoke. Whether it's an uncommonly smart network show that rewards careful viewing or a load of nonsense is in the eye of the beholder—but it remains one of the most discussed and debated highlights in TV history. Stream Lost on Disney+ and Hulu.

Kathryn Newton heads this surprisingly smart Lord of the Flies riff about a group of teenagers forced to create their own community after all the adults disappear and a dense fresh forest crops up around their small enclave, cutting them off from everything and everyone else. This one's about coming of age in a world where the usual rules are no longer in effect, and about how we're quick to reestablish an oppressive social order even when outside forces are no longer at work. Stream The Society on Netflix.

Black Friday scammers are targeting iPhones — turn on these iOS settings before you shop

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (452 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between back to back flash sales, urgent delivery updates, and constant order confirmations, Black Friday is prime hunting season for scammers trying to blend into a crowded inbox.
  • Taking two minutes to adjust a handful of built-in iOS protections puts an immediate barrier between your personal data and the most common holiday checkout traps, without slowing down your shopping.
  • Sources indicate that if your iPhone is running iOS 27, Apple’s newer anti-scam safeguard helps flag suspicious activity before money or account access changes hands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between back to back flash sales, urgent delivery updates, and constant order confirmations, Black Friday is prime hunting season for scammers trying to blend into a crowded inbox. Even cautious iPhone owners can get caught off guard when a fake package alert or spoofed bank warning lands right alongside real receipts.

Taking two minutes to adjust a handful of built-in iOS protections puts an immediate barrier between your personal data and the most common holiday checkout traps, without slowing down your shopping.

Sources indicate that if your iPhone is running iOS 27, Apple’s newer anti-scam safeguard helps flag suspicious activity before money or account access changes hands. Open Settings, Privacy & Security, Impersonation Risk Detection and turn on sharing with app developers.

When enabled, supported banking and shopping apps can receive risk signals (categorized as unknown, medium, or high) to pause or re-verify sensitive actions like payments, transfers, or password changes if someone is trying to coach you through a scam over the phone.

Recent findings suggest that scammers rely heavily on rapid-fire cold calls pretending to be fraud departments or tech support. Go to Settings, Accessibility, Audio & Visual, Call Audio Routing and double-check that Auto-Answer Calls is toggled off. Keeping it disabled ensures your iPhone will not accidentally pick up an incoming spam call on its own while connected to AirPods, headphones, or your car’s Bluetooth.

Sources indicate that fake courier texts claiming a missed delivery or unpaid customs fee surge during Black Friday weekend. Head to Settings, Apps, Messages, then scroll down to the Unknown Senders section, and toggle on both Screen Unknown Senders and Filter Spam.

Sources indicate that this sweeps suspicious texts out of your main inbox automatically. If you still want alerts for legitimate automated messages, such as two-factor login codes or time-sensitive delivery updates, tap Allow Notifications underneath and customize which categories can still buzz your screen.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level.
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level.
  • GTA 6 has no defined difficulty levels, which is in keeping with the franchise's tradition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally here, and one of the things people are talking about is the game's difficulty level. Some are saying it's too easy. Rockstar boss Rob Nelson has now entered the conversation, telling Destructoid that Rockstar's data highlighted that GTA 4 was "a little too punishing in places" and GTA 5 was "perhaps too easy." So with GTA 6, the team trying to "land somewhere in the middle." GTA 6 has no defined difficulty levels, which is in keeping with the franchise's tradition. That remarked, players can adjust things like aiming controls, while players can unlock cheat codes to make the game easier or harder. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dJDf76QVv70 Design producer Scott Mitchell, meanwhile, said the fail states in GTA 6 were designed to feel "appropriate." “We wanted to keep things open and not limit the players’ use of mechanics, such as stealth, but we did also want to make sure we retained the cinematic, high production value, explosive sequences that we’re known for, and people expect. It feels like we’ve managed to strike a good balance," he explained. Also in the interview, Nelson said figuring out the difficulty level for GTA 6 is itself challenging because the designers themselves know enemy positions better than anyone after playing and testing the game so much. "There’s a real process in unpicking some of that to create an experience most players will be able to enjoy, rather than endure," Nelson said. "The game is so massive, and has such a wide range of content that we can really lean into that, making certain open-world content--compounds and fronts for example---more difficult, to give players seeking a challenge something to sink their teeth into as well.” GTA 6 debuted on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U2 paid tribute to the late Dolly Parton with a posthumous duet at the NFL’s Thanksgiving Eve game.

The Irish rockers projected archival footage and audio of the country music icon for a hybrid live performance of their collaborative track “Torn” during halftime of the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams’ Wednesday, November 25, game at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

In between their ’80s hits “Sunday Bloody Sunday” and “Where the Streets Have No Name,” U2 joined a worldwide Netflix audience in celebrating the life and legacy of Parton, who died at age 80 in August following a brief battle with cancer.

“Torn” is thought to be the final song Parton recorded, having worked on the track with Bono in Nashville only two months before her death. The gripping ballad posits the hope of reconciliation in a family divided over their differences.

“I can’t deny this passion and desire / But I know it has to burn me standing this close to the fire,” Parton sings. “What am I supposed to do? And how am I supposed to choose? / I love ’em both, and I just feel so torn.”.

The track was officially released on U2’s 16th studio album, Carnaval de Luz, earlier this month. Parton shares a writing credit on “Torn” with U2 and Snow Patrol’s Johnny McDaid.

“When she got ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song,” Bono, 66, told Rolling Stone in August. “And you can hear that. And I can’t even listen to it now.”.

The musician revealed that he initially reached out to Parton about potentially collaborating on a completely separate project.

In a recent development, “She noted, ‘That’s a little too Irish for me,’” he recalled. “But she said, ‘I got this song. It’s called ‘Torn,’ and do you wanna see where you can take it somewhere else, maybe?’”.

U2 producer Garret “Jacknife” Lee told the outlet that Dolly “loved” the finished version of “Torn,” adding that she was “so proud of her vocal and the recording.”.

Recent findings suggest that “She was thrilled with it,” Lee, 59, noted. “We were very nervous that she might not approve or would be uncomfortable with it, but she loved it.”.

Bono remembered being blown away that Parton delivered such a powerful and haunting vocal performance considering her declining health at the time.

Sources indicate that “She sang her heart out, and I cannot believe that’s an 80-year-old woman,” Bono told Rolling Stone. “It’s very moving to have had these intimacies with such a figure. The fact that they’re not there now, in any way you can call back, other than through her songs, is very sobering.”.

According to recent reports, before the release of “Torn,” Parton’s most recent studio album, Rockstar, debuted in November 2023. That record featured rock collaborations with surviving Beatles Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr, Judas Priest frontman Rob Halford and even a cover of her goddaughter Miley Cyrus‘ hit “Wrecking Ball.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anyone still struggling to understand how Bernie Bros and MAGA voters overlap on the political Venn diagram might find answers in Ryan Grim’s audience.

In a recent development, grim, a veteran journalist and self-described “leftist,” has cultivated a rather politically diverse and incongruous fan base over his two decades in journalism. On election night in Los Angeles earlier this month, a room full of socialists erupted in cheers when Grim appeared on the major screen at the Democratic Socialists of America’s watch party (Grim was a guest that night on Hasan Piker’s livestream). The next day, a friend who religiously listens to Tim Dillon, a podcaster credited with helping Trump win reelection in 2024, and Tony Hinchcliffe, a comedian who performed at a Trump rally that same year, told me that he was also a huge fan of Grim’s.

According to recent reports, after working at Politico, HuffPost, and The Intercept, Grim, 48, cofounded Drop Site News, an independent nonprofit news organization, in 2024, and he’s also a cohost on the antiestablishment political podcast Breaking Points. He’s developed a reputation for being an equal opportunity critic of both parties, which Grim says helps explain why people all along the spectrum are attracted to his work. Even Steve Bannon (who called Grim an “intrepid reporter”) and former Republican congressman Matt Gaetz have occasionally thrown compliments his way.

It has been revealed that “I think there’s a huge overlap with Breaking Points, Drop Site, and the whole podcast-bro world,” Grim tells Vanity Fair. “It does feel like we’ve basically become the primary news source for the podcast bros, which is not how you would have necessarily understood the world several years ago.”.

But lest anyone think that Grim has changed his views to accommodate newly introduced fans, his frequent criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza has helped make him a target of Fox News host Mark Levin, who has called into question Drop Site’s nonprofit status.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Grim discusses his unlikely popularity among the podcast bros, why he thinks the Epstein files helped propel Democrats in 2026, why he doesn’t understand the protests against Jerry Seinfeld, and what his favorite jam band, Phish, taught him about tolerance.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

In a recent development, vanity Fair: You’ve talked about how being a leftist rather than a Democratic partisan has helped you build credibility with conservatives. Why is that distinction vital?

It has been revealed that ryan Grim: [The conservatives] never thought I was a Democratic partisan, because I wasn’t. I think if you have a view of the world, people are willing to say, Okay, that’s his view of the world, and I’m going to metabolize what he’s reporting while taking into account that he has a particular view of the world.

But if you’re a partisan for Democrats or Republicans, that’s different because then you’re playing, like, strategic games with your information, and your view of whether or not something is good or bad changes with whether or not it’s good or bad for Democrats or good or bad for Republicans, rather than being grounded in some type of idea about the world.

And you’ve been criticizing Democrats for decades.

Sources indicate that yeah, I think what frustrates our critics is that they can’t be like, “Oh yeah, well, you didn’t say that when Biden was president or when Obama was president,” and it’s like, “Oh no, in fact, we remarked this and worse,” because it didn’t matter the color of the jersey. We believed that drone strikes were wrong, or shutting down ACORN is bad, and we’re going to say it no matter who’s in office.

Jeremy [Scahill] and I have been doing this for so long that we have that track record, so I think that has really helped us build that audience across the spectrum. It’s been pretty gratifying to develop that conservative audience. It’s weird sometimes to hear a Steve Bannon or a Matt Gaetz applauding your journalism. But it’s like, hey, that doesn't necessarily mean they agree with us about our conclusions. That’s not what we’re here for. We’re here to do the reporting.

According to recent reports, you grew up around a lot of Moral Majority conservatives in rural Maryland, and you’ve said that even though you disagreed with their politics, you didn’t necessarily think they were bad people. Is that something the left has lost sight of?

They were almost universally pretty good people whose views I didn’t share as a young person and don’t now. But that’s just who they are.

I’ve talked to other people who still live in these rural areas, and they’re like, “How do I deal with these people who have these wretched beliefs?” I say, “Just deal with them as people.” They were kind of born believing that, and a lot of them are rethinking things all the time.

Industry observers note that you seem to have a lot more patience for people you disagree with than some of your fellow leftists. How do you reconcile that with your own pretty uncompromising politics?

Sources indicate that I try to live by the creed of [left-wing political commentator] Michael Brooks. He used to say, “Be ruthless to systems, be kind to people,” and that can be very hard. But to me the most crucial thing to do is try to understand that people operate within systems, and it is the system that you’re against, not the people.

I think you’re more likely to win converts by understanding what their role is in the system and keeping your criticisms at that systemic level.

I think sometimes people go a little bit crazy. I don’t agree with Jerry Seinfeld’s politics when it comes to Israel, but I don’t understand the value of protesting Jerry Seinfeld. Maybe he’s given some money or something, but like, in general, he’s not a decision-maker. What is the upside in making him a target of protest? That part I don’t understand.

Recent findings suggest that speaking of people who disagree with you, Mark Levin has been going after Drop Site News’s nonprofit status. How seriously are you taking his efforts?

So if tomorrow Levin succeeded, and we were no longer a nonprofit, we would then carry on as a for-profit supported by our readers.

Industry observers note that I know the underlying hostility is he doesn’t like our reporting—he doesn’t want it to exist. But stripping our nonprofit status wouldn’t change that. It would just turn it into a lucrative for-profit manufacturer, which I don’t understand. Like, that’s his preferred outcome? That we make a bunch of money doing this? I don’t think it’s very well thought through.

But couldn’t this become a much bigger problem for journalism? There are organizations like ProPublica and The Texas Tribune that could theoretically face similar attacks.

Yes, and certainly the Trump administration has been very publicly saying that it aims to go after the entire nonprofit complex, and everybody from Sierra Club on down, because they consider them to be political enemies.

But [the Trump administration] has also gotten a lot of pushback on this from the conservative-nonprofit world, which is actually much more lucratively funded than the progressive side, because the conservatives have mentioned [Democrats are] going to come for organizations like The Heritage Foundation when Republicans are no longer in power.

It has been revealed that let’s talk about the midterms. Moderates saw the blue wave as a vindication of the party’s affordability-focused strategy, while progressives saw it as a mandate for a more ambitious agenda. What was your biggest takeaway?

I think people are overlooking the role that the Epstein files and Trump’s cover-up, in particular, played. That was really a major break that eroded trust from his base and from independents.

In a recent development, we even did a survey right after he debuted the war and asked people if they thought he was going to war with Iran to distract, at least in part, from the Epstein scandal. And by a 50-to-42 margin, the majority of the country said yes, he is.

Whether true or not, the Epstein scandal bled into Iran, which then drove up gas prices and created all of this intense anxiety. Meanwhile, Trump is focused on the ballroom, which he’s using to collect bribes.

People believed when they elected him that he was going to drain the swamp, release the files, start no newly introduced wars, and focus instead on bringing down prices. That was what people understood he was going to do. And on all four, he just did the exact opposite, in, like, an aggressive, in-your-face, I-don’t-care-about-you kind of way.

You recently discussed a forensic expert’s analysis challenging the official account of Jeffrey Epstein’s death. What interested you about the coverage?

It was certainly interesting that The Upcoming York Times was willing to cover it.

In a recent development, their headline was funny. The one that the Times went with said something like, “Against Conventional Wisdom,” comma, “Forensic Expert Says Epstein Was Murdered.” And I was like, What? What conventional wisdom are you talking about here?

I don’t think the conventional wisdom was challenged there at all.

Sources indicate that we live in this interesting world where the public can get to, like, a 70-30, 80-20 belief in something without The Newly introduced York Times ever giving permission for that belief. And so then when they finally come around to it, like with this article, they say that the story they’re writing goes against conventional wisdom. The conventional wisdom may be wrong, but the conventional wisdom is that he was killed.

What does that say about the state of journalism?

The depressing part, from my perspective, is there’s almost nothing I can report anymore that our readers will admit they’re surprised by, and there’s pretty much nothing you could report on Epstein that would ever live up to what people just assume is true about him.

All right, something considerably more fun: We’re both Phish fans, and I’ve noticed a growing MAGA contingent at their concerts. Does that bother you?

Recent findings suggest that well, it’s the same audience. You know, they’re just going through changes in their lives. Doesn’t frustrate me at all. All are welcome.

I actually talked to Phish about this in 2002. I met the band after they played at Saturday Night Live. At the time, I was very agitated about the fact that they had not said anything about the Iraq war, and the drummer, Jon Fishman, told me they had said something, one political thing, several years earlier, and they just got flooded with letters from Republican fans who felt hurt.

According to recent reports, they’re like, You know what? We’re just not gonna go there anymore. Stop at a stop sign. This is about all we’re gonna say.

And you know what? It’s fine. We don’t need Phish to tell us what they think about the world. They can just create a space for us to think about it.

Phish would not have been able to stop the Iraq war.

But doesn’t some of the anti-Muslim and transphobic rhetoric on the right run counter to the ethos of Phish?

Yeah, but I don’t think any of their audience goes into that.

So you think they’re more fiscal conservatives?

In a recent development, yeah, yeah. These guys have done well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When discussing the best Batman, I'm pretty sure many people will say that Michael Keaton is #1, and I'm not going to disagree. Keaton OWNED that role. That remarked, is he the most interesting live-action version of the character? I'm going to say no.

In fact, I'm one of those weirdos who will acknowledge that while The Dark Knight is most people's favorite Batman movie, I'm actually of the opinion that Matt Reeves’ The Batman is the best Batman flick. That's all because of Robert Pattinson, who I think is the most fascinating version of Batman yet.

In a recent development, with confirmation that Pattinson is the new James Bond, I have a good feeling that he might also be the most interesting version of 007 yet. Here's why.

Industry observers note that while many people will likely say that Keaton is the best Batman, I think it's even more likely that most people will say that Sean Connery is the best Bond. Every subsequent Bond actor has unfortunately been judged against Connery, with many people saying that they liked Daniel Craig's bruiser Bond since he was a callback to the tough guy Bond that Connery represented.

Connery is also the reason why some people disregard Roger Moore's Bond, as some people think he verges too far into the silly territory. Personally, of all men who have played Bond, my favorite is Pierce Brosnan, but I respect those who prefer George Lazenby or Timothy Dalton.

That stated, I think Robert Pattinson, who I've already gone on record calling my favorite modern actor, will probably provide the most interesting take on the character yet. When trying to envision him as Bond, I think of his roles in Tenet, The Batman, and Primetime, all rolled into one. I see him being a subtler, quieter Bond than others (maybe closest to Dalton), and I'm looking forward to him creating his own version far removed from anything like Connery. Can you tell that I'm excited?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, one of the problems with reading Charles Schulz's Peanuts was the inconsistency among its collected editions.
  • There is a broad assortment​​​​​​​ of Peanuts comic collections on store and library shelves, of course.
  • In a recent development, some of this was reportedly due to Schulz himself, who exercised a lot of editorial control​​​​​​​ over which Peanuts strips were collected and where.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, one of the problems with reading Charles Schulz's Peanuts was the inconsistency among its collected editions. You'd think that Peanuts’ publishers, as the stewards of one of the most influential comic strips​​​​​​​ in the Western world, would simply reprint the comics in chronological order. It was rarely that simple.​​​​​​​.

There is a broad assortment​​​​​​​ of Peanuts comic collections on store and library shelves, of course. However, it's more common to find Peanuts books that feature themed selections, like 1985's baseball collection Significant League Peanuts. When you do find a straightforward collected edition of Peanuts, usually in secondhand stores, it often has a few conspicuous omissions. (They’re also usually 40- to 50-year-old books printed like dimestore novels, with yellowed paper and ink that’s started to flake off the pages​​​​​​​.).

In a recent development, some of this was reportedly due to Schulz himself, who exercised a lot of editorial control​​​​​​​ over which Peanuts strips were collected and where. Specifically, Schulz is the reason why it was so difficult for so long to find official reprints of Peanuts' first few years, as he apparently regarded the strip's early days as something of an old shame.

That didn't change until 2004, when the Seattle indie comics publisher Fantagraphics began to release The Complete Peanuts, a 26-volume series that features the comic's full run in chronological order. Even if you're familiar with Schulz's work, there are likely a few surprises waiting for you somewhere in The Complete Peanuts, as quite a bit of Peanuts was voluntarily thrown down the memory hole. Unless you were lucky enough to grow up right alongside the comic’s initial publication, there are a few Peanuts strips in the full collection that even a superfan may not have seen.

It can also highlight how some characters entered the strip almost fully formed. Charlie Brown's little sister Sally doesn't have quite the same evolutionary arc as the rest of the Peanuts gang. Once she was old enough to go to school, it rapidly became both her literal friend and her worst enemy.

It has been revealed that sally was first introduced in May 1959 and spent​​​​​​​ her first few appearances as an infant before being allowed to accelerate into childhood. Sally started kindergarten in 1962 and remained roughly the same age for the rest of the strip’s run.​​​​​​​.

As you read through The Complete Peanuts, many of Sally's running jokes and character tics appear surprisingly early.​​​​​​​ Her one-sided crush on Linus goes back to 1960, and her ambivalence towards both school and life more broadly is visible by the 1970s. Charlie Brown may rage against the unfairnesses of the world and Linus may be stoic about them, but Sally looks at them as if through the eyes of a nihilistic French philosopher. They don't matter, because nothing matters.

According to recent reports, that helps to explain Sally's general attitude towards school, which is one of the most consistent elements of her character over the course of 40 years​​​​​​​. Sally would rather tell a story than learn a fact, which applies whether she's practicing basic skills or making a presentation in front of the class. She simply inhabits a different, stranger world than most of the people around her.

In the Sunday strip for Jan. 19, 1975, Sally gets up in front of her class to deliver a report on rock snakes, which she presents with a cadence suitable for network television. The look on her face in the fourth panel is what really sold this for me, as it's one of the most manic grins Schulz ever drew​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that "What, you may ask, is a rock snake? That is a good question! A rock snake is a snake that sneaks up behind you, and throws a rock at you!" Sally tells her class. "Now, here is my exclusive... it used to be thought that rock snakes were dangerous, but my authority says this is not so...".

This is, of course, all nonsense, although it's fun to think of how a snake would pick up and throw a rock. I imagine it works something like a slingshot.

The punchline is that Sally has apparently based her entire report on something Linus told her, which is a little out of character for him, but maybe he was simply trying to scare Sally at the time. However it shook out​​​​​​​, Sally's rock snake report is going to be on my mind whenever I see someone else trying to fake their way through an assignment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My elderly mom, who has been deeply unwell for a number of years, has recently started clenching her hands into balls and curling her feet inward like little hooks. Her gerontologist noted that, horribly enough, her mind is no longer sending a message to her body that she needs to relax. Medicine can’t help, she explained, but massage might. So one evening, I turned to Google Maps, where I increasingly find everything from authentic Thai restaurants to the best place to buy youth soccer cleats. I guided the map app to the Upper West Side, one of the country’s most expensive neighborhoods, and put one word in the search bar: “massage.”.

It has been revealed that then I squinted. Why was the massage table at “Ashley massage and spa” lit by dark purple light? And why did another listing have photos of the masseuse herself in skin-tight exercise wear, with directions to contact her on Telegram? But it all became clearer when I spotted a description of the type of massage services offered: “I’m available for deep tissue, Swedish, or any kind of massage appointment with a happy ending.”.

Sources indicate that even if nothing should surprise us anymore about our tech overlords, I was still pretty shocked to find that Google Maps appeared to be the fresh Craigslist, famous for its battle with regulators over sex work classifieds. Somewhere between figuring out the location of the neighborhood CVS and “coffee near me,” it seems like Google branched out. I’d always assumed it adhered to local laws—sex work is illegal in New York state—but perhaps Silicon Valley’s fave “we’re just a platform not a publisher” defense applied here. Otherwise, why on earth was the algorithm retrieving sex work listings when I was just trying to help my 84-year-old mom?

I emailed Google PR to ask what, exactly, was going on, giving them a deadline of the next day to respond.

It has been revealed that the response came from a senior publicist, quickly. “Hi Vanessa - I'm on the Google Comms team. Would you be able to provide the listings and screenshots?”.

In a recent development, I did so, then received another response: “I’m reviewing all of this, but wondering if you have wiggle room in your deadline? Want to make sure I can get you the right info in time, and I think that timing tomorrow may be challenging.”.

I responded that I could wait until a couple more days to find out what Google had to say.

In the meantime, I contacted some experts.

In a recent development, mike Blumenthal has been studying Google Maps almost since it existed. A co-founder of Near Media, he began writing about the product in 2005 and states he first documented large-scale spam on Maps in Latest York City in 2009. When I demonstrated him the strange massage listings I’d found scattered across New York, he wasn’t particularly surprised. Google Maps is an extraordinarily valuable way to get in front of customers, which gives gray and black market businesses a powerful incentive to game it. Once they figure out how to convince Google’s algorithm that real people should be directed to those listings, “they can make bank.”.

Google removes an enormous amount of fake listings, reviews and images, and has tightened its verification procedures over the years, said Blumenthal. But when those systems fail, enforcement is largely reactive. Even Blumenthal, who has volunteered in Google’s forums for nineteen years and knows how to escalate a complaint, said getting suspicious listings removed can take upwards of a month or six weeks. When a problem attracts press attention, though, he notes Google can act within hours. What Google doesn’t do, in his view, is spend enough to prevent the same problems from recurring. “They won’t put in place systemic fixes. They won’t put in place people to deal with this quickly…They don’t want the cost.”.

After I talked to Blumenthal, I read the reviews of some of the massage businesses that Google Maps was serving up nationwide. Not all were positive. One reviewer of the “Asian Palace Spa” in San Francisco, writing five years ago, gave the business one star and called it a “fraud,” saying he had paid for an hour-long massage but received only 15 minutes before being asked for additional money for “extra services.” The review had received 17 likes. Another one-star reviewer from the same period remarked, “they don’t have spa, just pay for room and then pay for lady for whatever you do.”.

According to recent reports, but many more of the illicit massage businesses had positive reviews, about services that were above and beyond, with smiley kissy face icons attached. Were these just independent sex workers trying to make a living? Was it so wrong that they were using Google Maps to find clients? Perhaps it’s needless to say, but when I called several of the phone numbers and introduced myself as a reporter, information was not forthcoming.

Industry observers note that I started to feel a little queasy as I reviewed a listing that was clearly written by a woman working for herself, just trying to make a listing. But then, as I looked more closely at others, I realized that the photos were so similar, and the setups of the listings so close to each other, that they must be coordinated by an organized group. Whether that was a lead-generator for escorts who needed extra clients, or a scammer, or a sex trafficker, I couldn’t tell.

In a recent development, I searched for illicit massage listings in different cities, and found them all over neighborhoods in Los Angeles, from Beverly Hills to Koreatown. I also began to notice that most of the massage spots seemed as though they were unlikely to actually be located in the spots they claimed to be. For example, a masseuse who appeared to be nude from breastbone up, with a butterfly tattoo decorating her clavicle, located her business on the Upper East Side’s Museum Mile, home to multimillion dollar apartments and New York’s great cultural institutions, but she also included information about a certain corner in Queens, where it seemed like she could’ve also set up shop.

Recent findings suggest that now that I had more information, I tried to understand whether Google Maps bore any responsibility for these listings, calling Chelsea Binns, a professor at John Jay College of Criminal Justice who studies cybercrime. “It’s interesting from an anti-fraud perspective, because we rely on Google Maps virtually every day now,” she remarked, taking the call from Japan. “No one takes out a hard map anymore. And there’s a bit of borrowed credibility, because these listings are on Google. It’s Google Maps!”.

In a recent development, despite this, Binns indicates responsibility rests with each individual user to decipher the legitimacy of a Google Maps business, a caveat emptor situation. “A lot of us don’t read disclaimers, but somewhere deep within the service it says they’re not at fault,” explains Binns. “It’s ‘use at your own risk, research independently, and verify.’”.

“But why don’t they care if it’s an illegal service?” I ask. “They wouldn’t have guns on there.”.

It has been revealed that “They do care,” says Binns. “They actively review their content. I suspect this slipped through the cracks. But at some point you’re just playing whack-a-mole. You take one down, and another pops up.”.

Industry observers note that this was the perspective of AI-critic Brian Merchant, creator of the Blood in the Machine podcast and newsletter. “As [Google] has moved their resources into moderating, training, and shipping AI, I would not be surprised if resources that were dedicated to moderating are falling off, and things are just staying up longer,” he notes. “And maybe criminal organizations have been emboldened, realizing that they can get their links listed higher and longer, and it’ll be weeks before they’re taken down.”.

Recent findings suggest that but the next time I checked out the massage listings near my mom’s apartment, almost all had disappeared. And I heard back from Google with a statement: “Google Maps only displays places that people can visit or interact with in the real world, and we've removed the businesses that do not exist at these locations.”.

This seemed to indicate that Google had taken action to remove listings in my mom’s neighborhood, and that I was also correct when I noticed that some of the sex workers weren’t actually in the locations they said they were. Google also directed me to their policies against adult-themed content, which explain that no one uploading listings can violate local laws, especially in the areas of “alcohol, gambling, tobacco, guns, health and medical devices, regulated pharmaceuticals, adult services, and financial services.”.

A Google spokesperson further pushed back against Mike Blumenthal’s contention that the firm doesn’t want to incur costs monitoring Google Maps, noting, “we placed posting restrictions on more than 782,000 policy-violating accounts and removed over 13 million fake Business Profiles, further defending genuine businesses on Maps. We blocked or removed over 292 million policy-violating reviews, while publishing more than 1 billion helpful reviews.” Google also added, “we hold bad actors accountable through account suspension and litigation. We display alerts to let you know if we've recently removed suspicious five-star reviews in certain circumstances. These warnings help you understand quickly if a place may be engaging in unfair review practices.”.

They also directed me to their policies against adult-themed content, which explain that no one uploading listings can violate local laws, especially in the areas of “alcohol, gambling, tobacco, guns, health and medical devices, regulated pharmaceuticals, adult services, and financial services.”.

I contacted Danielle Citron, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law, to understand more. She mentioned that Google’s statement made sense. “Ordering, filtering, and otherwise structuring the presentation of content” is likely to be shielded as “publishing and speaking” under Section 230, the law that protects tech platforms from liability for user-uploaded content, she said. But there could be a wrinkle. “A different question is getting paid for and designing systems in a particular way, [which] may not be immunized,” she explains, mentioning social media cases like Fresh Mexico v. Meta, “where [a lawsuit challenging platform design] was permitted to go to trial because it was about what Meta did in their design of sites, not what users did to kids.” So a question could potentially be asked by attorneys in the future along these lines: Is the very structure of Google Maps allowing gray and black market businesses to flourish?

It has been revealed that within a week, some listings that Google removed when I last checked seemed to have popped up in Latest York again, but there were far less of them. Still, I found it confounding that in trying to find a massage for my mom, I had uncovered a network of massage spots that a less savvy consumer than myself might have imagined were legitimate. “We really need a better understanding of this landscape, because we need to look out for the consumer,” Binns told me. “Your mom is someone who is vulnerable in society, and that can take many forms. She’s perhaps incapable of doing the due diligence that’s required just to get an ordinary service.”.

At the same time, I was aware that no one wants to change Google’s algorithm to the point that it screws over legitimate small businesses that rely on the visibility of Google Maps. Blumenthal explained the conundrum to me this way: if Google tightens their mapping search controls too much, “businesses’ reality becomes worse, because you can’t get into [Maps]. If they loosen it, consumers’ reality becomes worse, because shit gets in.”.

Sources indicate that after all of this back and forth, I still had to solve my initial problem: securing a massage for my mom. I contacted a few spots in her neighborhood that looked legitimate, but they mentioned she’d have to raise herself on the massage table, which, since she’s in a wheelchair, wouldn’t work. I decided to reach out to her Medicare-supplied occupational therapist, who got back to me right away.

In a recent development, he said he’d been meaning to call. He needed to send me a form saying that my mom was no longer able to participate in the exercises they were performing together, and she’d likely be kicked off Medicare payment for them in the near future. That was a bummer, and made me regret calling him at all, but I figured while I had him on the line I’d ask another question: Does Medicare (original, parts A & B) cover therapeutic massage? He said no, apologetically.

I’d spent a week investigating a system that made it remarkably easy to sell massages that weren't massages, only to discover how difficult it was to obtain one that was.

If You Loved 'Cupertino,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, cupertino is one of those TV demonstrates that arrived just when we all needed it.
  • Recent findings suggest that just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not.
  • According to recent reports, at its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, cupertino is one of those TV demonstrates that arrived just when we all needed it. In this economy, a story about two lawyers who get shafted by the “move fast and break things” culture of Silicon Valley and decide to use their legal chops to fight back was almost destined to be a hit, and the great performances by Mike Colter and Rachel Keller sealed the deal. If you love the sharp legal wrangling and tech-focused storylines and want a movie that perfectly complements the show, it’s time to watch (or re-watch) Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher’s 2010 masterpiece, The Social Network.

Recent findings suggest that just like Cupertino, The Social Network arrived at precisely the right moment in history—just when everyone was beginning to wonder if the social media revolution kicked off by Facebook and Mark Zuckerberg was actually a good idea or not. While it might seem hard to imagine, there was a time when Facebook was the social media platform—everyone was on it, and it dominated the conversation like nothing else. And the outsized wealth and influence Zuckerberg accrued as a result were just starting to make people a little uneasy.

According to recent reports, at its core, The Social Network is a legal drama—the framing narrative involves dual lawsuits brought against Zuckerberg and the depositions he is giving, which prompt flashbacks to the formation and success of Facebook in the early 2000s. Like Cupertino, the story is soaked in the “apologize later” culture of tech startups, and traces the ruthlessness and cold genius of Zuckerberg as he cements his control over the platform, ices out former partners, and generally behaves like a sociopathic genius (Jesse Eisenberg’s performance as Zuckerberg is coldly compelling).

The film doesn’t have any kind of clear-cut ending where the good guys win, but there’s a certain satisfaction in the way Sorkin’s script and Eisenberg’s performance strip away the glamour of Zuckerberg’s money and success, reducing him in many ways to an aggrieved loner who translated his rage into a brilliant idea, and then has to isolate himself from everyone in order to maintain his control over it. The Zuckerberg depicted in the film is a lonely, bitter dude, and it’s as much of a happy ending as you’ll get. It’s a fascinating story of legal maneuvering and bickering lawyers against a backdrop of one of the foundational social media moments that shaped modern culture, and fans of the show will dig it. Stream The Social Network on Pluto or rent it on Prime Video.

Still craving legal drama, tech-sector skulduggery, or more David-versus-Goliath courtroom fireworks? Here are a few more movies that fans of Cupertino will love.

Recent findings suggest that it’s set nowhere near Silicon Valley, but Michael Clayton is a real barn-burner of a paranoid legal thriller. George Clooney plays the title role, a “fixer” for a big-money law firm. When his mentor and friend, Arthur Edens (Tom Wilkinson), suffers a mental breakdown while working on a case involving a toxic weedkiller produced by one of the firm’s clients and becomes a security threat, he’s assassinated, and Clayton is forced to reckon with his role in the world and how much injustice he’s willing to tolerate in exchange for money. It’s tense, smart, and has a wonderfully satisfying conclusion that fans of legal dramas where the good guys are willing to sacrifice (and win) will cheer. Rent Michael Clayton on Prime Video.

Based on real events, Dark Waters will appeal to anyone who likes to see smart lawyers take on enormous corporations in a search for the truth. A successful corporate lawyer, Robert Bilott (Mark Ruffalo), looks into a series of bizarre cattle deaths in rural West Virginia and stumbles onto evidence that the DuPont corporation has been dumping illegal, unregulated chemicals into the groundwater. Bilott’s years-long effort to hold DuPont responsible for the health impact on the community nearly costs him everything, but his determination to make the system work is ultimately the kind of inspiring legal story fans of Cupertino will appreciate. Rent Dark Waters on Prime Video.

If you just want the simple pleasures of a thrilling legal procedural, you can’t do much better than A Civil Action. John Travolta (at the height of his comeback) plays attorney Jan Schlichtmann, who takes on a class action lawsuit against two huge corporations because he thinks the case will be lucrative and relatively straightforward. As the case saps his resources and brings his firm to the brink of collapse, however, Schlichtmann slowly realizes that he’s fighting for more than just a substantial payday. Fair warning: This isn’t a feel-good movie in many ways, but it definitely brings those David-versus-Goliath vibes that Cupertino trades in. Rent A Civil Action on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, the true story behind the effort to license the video game Tetris from the Soviet-era Russian government doesn’t have the same stakes as many of the stories in Cupertino, and it’s certainly no longer timely. But the globe-trotting legal maze that Henk Rogers (Taron Egerton) must navigate to secure the rights, which seem to keep twisting and slipping from his grasp as various political and corporate interests weigh in, is just as fun and fascinating as the legal battles on the show. Tetris may no longer be a novel sensation in the gaming world, but it’s fascinating to see how something so baked into modern pop culture achieved that status. Stream Tetris on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that if your favorite part of Cupertino is its exploration of the way tech companies impact our lives, and the way decisions made in obscure corporate offices can have enormous consequences, BlackBerry will be a favorite. Based on true events, it tells the story of how Research in Motion (RIM) created what was, for a time, the most dominant phone in the world—and how the company lost everything when its leaders took their eye off the ball and let personal obsessions and grudges impede their work. With a cast that includes Jay Baruchel and Glenn Howerton, this story of Silicon Valley hubris is right on target for Cupertino fans. Stream Blackberry on Netflix, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

Another Gaming Console Price Hike Could Be Coming, Thanks To New Tariffs

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the US government has announced a new round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • It has been revealed that the US government has unveiled a upcoming round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners.
  • Sources indicate that what does this mean for gaming hardware?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the US government has announced a new round of tariffs targeting several major countries, including China, Japan, Vietnam, and European Union trading partners. Under the proposed tariffs, import taxes will rise significantly, with China facing up to 40% when the new duties take effect next year. According to the BBC, some of the rates will be reduced because of tariff caps that US President Donald Trump has already agreed to, and individual countries could also face different levies. What does this mean for gaming hardware? Trump's first round of "Liberation Day" tariffs contributed to rising console prices, but the Supreme Court eventually struck them down. Major companies like Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo benefited from tariff refunds after the ruling, but they didn't pass the savings on to consumers. In Sony's case, it was estimated to get back $508 million in refunds from the US government. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4FatSqS3VYY&t=19s The new tariffs bypass the Supreme Court's ruling by using a different law, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the government to impose tariffs on countries that use unfair business practices. The law does require an investigation into specific trade practices before rates are set. If higher import taxes take effect, console companies could face much higher costs, and protecting their profits will likely mean consumers have to cover the difference. Nintendo, Sony, and Microsoft have moved much of their final assembly out of China and into Southeast Asia, especially Vietnam, to avoid earlier tariffs. However, key parts like batteries and power supplies still mostly come from China, and if tariffs on these parts rise, total production costs for consoles made outside China will go up even more. Some electronic goods could be exempt from tariffs, and manufacturers often stockpile inventory ahead of tariff deadlines to delay price changes. But with rising costs from the ongoing components shortage amid the AI boom and other global factors, console prices remain at risk. After the June announcement of steep console price hikes, Microsoft warned that Xbox console costs could rise again in 2027, and next-gen hardware is also expected to be very pricey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that one of the most talked-about characters in GTA 6 outside of Jason and Lucia has been Mandy, a woman who tries to seduce Jason early in the game. She may also be a serial killer. The actor who plays Mandy, Lexie Shoaibi, has now discussed how she got the part and her reaction to people being weird online. Speaking to Vulture, Shoaibi stated she's able to see "more good than bad" thanks to her experience being a content creator. "There are weirdos out there, and they’re going to try to bring you down, so it’s important to stay around the people and the places that aren’t doing that," she said. "It’s easy enough to do, which I’m very grateful for. There’s enough support in my real-life community and online that I can say, 'I could just hang out over here. I don’t actually need to go to the scary place.' I’m living in the positive, for sure." https://www.youtube.com/shorts/JSJwQthWrZs People have been, to put it mildly, thirsting over Mandy since GTA 6 came out. However, Shoaibi had no idea she was going to be in GTA 6 at all because when she auditioned, she signed what she described as an "incredibly" strict NDA. In fact, she didn't even know what she was auditioning for. Her commercial agent in New York brought it to her, and she thought it would be "just like any other commercial audition." From the time she auditioned until the game released on November 19, Shoaibi did not know she was going to be in GTA 6. Instead, she did the audition and recorded her scenes for a project she knew as "Project Bubblegum." Shoaibi said the notes she received included being told to play a “sexy ex-girlfriend" and to "be seductive.”  When Shoaibi finally saw Mandy in GTA 6, she said it was "very exciting," in part because it meant that Rockstar didn't cut it. She did the recording for Mandy in 2023 or early 2024, Shoaibi said, and now that GTA 6 is finally here and her role as Mandy confirmed, Shoaibi said, "I feel like I'm living in a dream. It's crazy." Shoaibi said she hopes her role as Mandy in the biggest video game ever can help grow her profile and get more jobs. "There’s definitely momentum that I wasn’t feeling before," she said. GTA 6 launched on November 19 and had a gigantic debut, selling 32.5 million copies by launch and generating around $4 billion on day one. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Voice alum Josh Sanders has been jailed in North Carolina following a recent arrest.

Us can confirm that Sanders, 38, is being held without bond at Concord, North Carolina’s Cabarrus County Jail following a Wednesday, November 25, arrest on suspicion of driving while impaired and communicating threats.

Sanders is scheduled to address the accusations in court on February 3, 2027.

The musician was booked into Cabarrus County Jail by officers of the Kannapolis Police Department on Wednesday when he refused to consent to a breathalyzer or blood test during a traffic stop, per People. (TMZ was the first to report the arrest.).

The outlet reported that Sanders is not currently eligible for bond because he was already on pretrial release for a separate case involving multiple alleged traffic violations.

He was allegedly accused of driving recklessly and possessing a revoked registration plate in a warrant issued on August 19. Court records obtained by People indicated that Sanders was charged with resisting a public officer, allowing an uninsured vehicle to be operated, failing to maintain liability insurance and violating a license plate frame or cover restriction, as well as having an improper muffler.

Sanders allegedly posted a $2,000 bond to secure his release following his August 29 arrest.

Industry observers note that it is not known whether Sanders has legal representation. He has not made any comment about his recent legal trouble.

Sanders made it all the way to the finals of The Voice season 25 in May 2024 before finishing as runner-up to eventual winner, Asher HaVon.

According to recent reports, the Kannapolis, North Carolina, native initially won over Voice coach Reba McEntire with his cover of Nate Smith‘s Billboard No. 1 Country hit “Whiskey On You” during The Voice‘s Blind Auditions round in February 2024.

Sanders later brought McEntire, 71, to tears during rehearsals for the Battle Rounds when he shared his deeply personal connection to Luke Combs‘ “When It Rains It Pours,” which he was to perform alongside fellow contestant Donny Van Slee.

“‘When it rains, it pours,’ that lyric kind of hits me a little heavier,” he confided in McEntire. “I’m a dad of four. We had a son. He was born and passed away on my birthday. It’s such a fun song, man, and I don’t want to take it there.”.

McEntire offered Sanders advice on how to get through the track, nearly choking up while explaining that she asks “the Holy Spirit to walk for me, talk for me, sing for me” before every live performance.

Diablo 4 Is Making Helltides A Hell Of A Lot Easier

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of Diablo 4's oldest endgame activities, Helltides, is getting a major refresh for Season 16.

  • Industry observers note that as detailed by developer Blizzard in their full breakdown of Season of Tyrael's Gambit, Helltides will soon be far more efficient to run than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Diablo 4's oldest endgame activities, Helltides, is getting a major refresh for Season 16. As detailed by developer Blizzard in their full breakdown of Season of Tyrael's Gambit, Helltides will soon be far more efficient to run than before. The whole point of the activity is to kill as many demons as fast as possible, acquire the Aberrant Cinders they drop, and then use those cinders to open chests for items. Dying means losing half of the cinders you've collected, but they are also lost when the Helltide ends. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beowulf is one of the oldest surviving pieces of English literature, and its story of a hero defending the Danes from a monster has inspired numerous adaptations.
  • It has been revealed that howard McCain’s 2008 film Outlander has no relationship to the megahit time-travel romance series.
  • Industry observers note that the film doesn’t waste too much time with exposition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beowulf is one of the oldest surviving pieces of English literature, and its story of a hero defending the Danes from a monster has inspired numerous adaptations. John McTiernan told the story in his 1999 film The 13th Warrior, and Robert Zemeckis used motion capture for a 2007 version. But my favorite telling of the story eschews history and fantasy to turn the tale of Beowulf and Grendel into an Alien-inspired sci-fi action flick.

It has been revealed that howard McCain’s 2008 film Outlander has no relationship to the megahit time-travel romance series. It was an enormous flop, earning only $7 million on an estimated budget of $47 million, and was panned by critics for being a derivative genre mashup with wooden performances. Those complaints are certainly fair, but Outlander also brings a surprising amount of depth and pathos to its absurd premise.

Industry observers note that the film doesn’t waste too much time with exposition. In the year 709 AD, Kainan (Jim Caviezel) crashes on Earth, a seed colony abandoned by his militaristic spacefaring people. That explains why he looks human and can quickly learn the local Norse dialect. The accident was caused by a stowaway, a monstrous alien known as a Moorwen. Now it’s on the loose, slaughtering Vikings, and causing chaos in an already fraught political situation. Kainan has to explain the threat in terms the locals can understand, so he claims to be hunting a dragon.

According to recent reports, outlander borrows heavily from both the Alien franchise and The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers. The legendary actor John Hurt brings some genuine gravitas to the aging king Rothgar of Heorot, who is trying to secure his people’s future by marrying his daughter Freya (Sophia Myles) to Wulfric (Jack Huston), a hotheaded warrior very clearly modeled after Karl Urban’s Éomer. Freya is a reasonably compelling blend of Eowyn and Ripley, getting revenge on the toothy monster that drools all over her by hacking it to death with a sword.

The Moorwen first strikes a neighboring village with a longstanding rivalry with Heorot, and Rothgar is more afraid of reprisals than the actual monster. The three-way conflict leads to a series of tense, chaotic fight scenes. A party involving a drinking game where Kainan and Wulfric balance on shields held by other warriors while chugging mead and doing sick flips is interrupted by raiders. After a few skirmishes, Ron Perlman’s King Gunnar bursts onto the scene like a video game boss swinging around two maces and nearly killing Rothgar. After Gunnar is pushed back, the Moorwen attacks.

Industry observers note that the CGI isn’t great, but McCain makes the most of the limitations by relying on smoke, shadows, and some clever creature design. The Moorwen looks a lot like a glowing displacer beast from Dungeons & Dragons, using its whiplike tail to grapple and decapitate Vikings in ludicrous gouts of blood. Bioluminescence ominously foreshadows the Moorwen's approach and makes it look decidedly alien rather than like a fantastical beast.

According to recent reports, the Moorwen also has a surprisingly sympathetic backstory. It’s not just a mindless killing machine but a survivor of a genocide Kainan helped carry out to create a new colony for his people. The scenes of its planet being firebombed and bulldozers sweeping piles of bones into mass graves speak to the same idea of humans as evil alien invaders that James Cameron would use in Avatar just a year later, albeit with much better special effects.

According to recent reports, outlander keeps its fights fresh with a strong mix of environments and tactics. The game of shields is introduced as a fun diversion but then plays a critical role in a trap laid for the Moorwen. The beast’s lair is an appropriately spooky volcanic cave, which both makes sense geographically and really adds to the alien dragon vibe. Dan Trachtenberg made Vikings fight a Predator as part of his 2025 film Predator: Killer of Killers, but Outlander did it first — and better — since its Vikings always feel at an enormous disadvantage, even with Kainan’s knowledge to help them.

Beowulf is a tragedy, but while Outlander is full of death, Kainan gets a happy ending in the form of a fresh start. Likewise, the film deserves a shot at redemption. It’s far from perfect, but it’s a highly entertaining and ambitious retelling of a classic offering fantasy and sci-fi fans something to love.

Outlander is available to rent from Prime Video, Apple TV, and other VOD services.

#132585. Lucia’s Rise: ‘Grand Theft Auto’ Forces Gamers to Grow Up—and Punishes Them With Narrative Consequences If They Refuse

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1840 w)
