💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you picked up a newly introduced iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started.
  • According to recent reports, ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile.
  • If someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you picked up a newly introduced iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo this fall, or you’re shopping for someone with an iPad, AirPods, or Apple Watch, there’s a good chance you’ve been holding out on purchasing accessories until all of the Black Friday deals started. We’ve got you covered with some great deals on premium accessories for nearly every Apple device on your list.

According to recent reports, ESR has been making Apple accessories since 2009, and that track record has made it a trustworthy name for the more than 123 million people who use its products to protect their Apple devices and make them more versatile. Here’s a look at what’s included in ESR’s Black Friday lineup and who each one is for.

If someone on your shopping list picked up an iPhone Duo, a case is the first thing they need, and it’s also the hardest one to get right. As we’ve seen with Android foldables, you’re protecting two halves, a hinge, and a phone that changes shape throughout the day as you use it, all without adding bulk to a device people bought because it folds thin. ESR has two options for iPhone Duo owners, and the choice mostly comes down to the look you want to achieve.

Sources indicate that the ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand is your choice if you want to show off your iPhone Duo’s colors. It combines a rigid polycarbonate and acrylic back with a softer TPU frame. The rigid back keeps the case from flexing and lets the iPhone Duo’s design show through, while the flexible frame absorbs the shock if you drop it (please don’t).

In a recent development, the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. It’s made from organic silicone leather with a soft, skin-friendly feel and a stain-resistant finish. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually shows every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

In a recent development, both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR claims it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

Both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

The same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

It has been revealed that on these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

Protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case is up to 28% off, and the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case is up to 37% off.

In a recent development, A case protects everything except the part you touch all day. The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the name is worth unpacking. Armorite is ESR’s line of toughened screen protectors, and the Pro version is made with Accessory Glass by Corning™. Corning has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone, so in non-tech speak, this is glass from a trustworthy name rather than generic tempered glass.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: ESR says the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing indicates up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

It has been revealed that installation is the part most people dread on a brand-new iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Black Friday deal: The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector is 15% off.

Holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and remarked it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

According to recent reports, it’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR says it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to 50% in about 15 minutes. It’s also TÜV-certified, meaning an independent testing organization has verified its safety features.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger is up to 32% off from November 20 through December 1.

For the student or anyone who does real work on an iPad, the ESR Shift Keyboard Case makes for an incredible gift. The Bluetooth keyboard attaches magnetically and comes off when you don’t need it, so you can type an essay at a desk, then pull the keyboard away to watch something on the couch or sketch with the iPad flat on a table.

Sources indicate that ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

Industry observers note that the trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

The ESR Shift Keyboard Case comes in versions for iPad Pro 11-inch and 13-inch (M4 and M5), iPad Air 11-inch and 13-inch (including the fresh M4 models), and iPad (A16), so whichever iPad you’re trying to take to the next level of productivity, there’s a Shift that fits it.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Shift Keyboard Case is up to 25% off, depending on your iPad model.

Have you ever dropped your AirPods case and watched the earbuds go flying? With the Cyber FlickLock, you won’t have to worry about that. We’ve covered FlickLock in MagSafe Monday before, but let’s recap it.

In a recent development, when the internal latch is engaged, the magnets line up to attract each other and hold the lid shut with maximum force, adding a second layer of security. Slide the button, and the magnets shift to repel each other, so the lid pops open with one hand. ESR claims the slide mechanism has been tested over 20,000 times.

The result is that your AirPods stay in the case if you drop it. Both cases also have 260g of magnetic strength, so they snap onto MagSafe chargers, Apple Watch chargers, and MagSafe batteries if you need to charge your AirPods. Again, it’s extremely strong, but extremely easy to unlock with one hand.

It has been revealed that the ESR Cyber FlickLock Magnetic Case is extremely durable and has a clip hook, so you can hang your AirPods on a backpack while hiking or cycling. The ESR Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Case brings the same lock in a range of vibrant colors with a carrying lanyard, so you can wear your AirPods on your wrist or attach them to a bag. Both cases come in versions for AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2 and 1, and AirPods 5 and 4. No matter which AirPods you or your loved one have, this is the case everyone will love.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Cyber FlickLock and Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Cases are both 20% off.

The ESR Equinox Watch Band is a quick pick for anyone who works out in the morning while tracking progress with Apple Watch, then heads to the office. A pin-and-fold lock keeps it secure, and it’s made from HNBR, a durable, skin-friendly synthetic rubber that resists water and tearing, with ventilation cutouts for all-day comfort. It fits 44mm, 45mm, 46mm, and 49mm models across Apple Watch Ultra 1 through 4, Series 4 through 12, and SE 1 through 3, and it comes in several colors to match your outfit or your mood that day.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Equinox Watch Band is 20% off.

The best gifts are the ones that get used every day, and accessories are the part of the Apple experience people live with the most. A case that props up a foldable, a screen protector made with Corning glass, a charger with a built-in cable, and an AirPods case that stays closed even when dropped check all the boxes. ESR truly makes something for everyone and is one of the most trusted names in the Apple accessories ecosystem.

ESR built its Black Friday lineup around the whole Apple ecosystem, from the upcoming iPhone Duo to iPad, AirPods, and even a great Apple Watch band, with premium materials and versatile designs that are durable, functional, and great-looking. ESR’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals run on Amazon from November 19 through November 30 (the Xtend 45W runs through December 1), with discounts of up to 37%!

Be sure to follow ESR on X and Facebook to keep up with all of its latest products, deals, and more.

Critical Role Officially Confirms a Fan-Favorite Episode Format Will Not Return

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the best things about Critical Role’s live highlights is that, in many ways, they're a phenomenal way to address story threads the cast couldn’t get to by the end of the campaign.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, it isn’t all story-based.
  • In a recent development, that being said, not all of these one-shot Dungeons & Dragons adventures are created equal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of the best things about Critical Role’s live highlights is that, in many ways, they're a phenomenal way to address story threads the cast couldn’t get to by the end of the campaign. For example, The Mighty Nein Reunion: Echoes of the Solstice 2023 live show is set shortly after the Apogee Solstice, an event primarily associated with Campaign 3: Bells Hells but also directly affecting The Mighty Nein adventuring group, particularly Beauregard Lionett and Caleb Widogast.

Recent findings suggest that however, it isn’t all story-based. There have been plenty of wacky shenanigans at the live shows too, such as PvP in2025’s Total Party Kill and 2026’s Projekt Funball.

In a recent development, that being said, not all of these one-shot Dungeons & Dragons adventures are created equal. In the most recent episode of Fireside Chat, Critical Role co-founder and creative director Marisha Ray made it crystal clear that there is a particular D&D one-shot idea she would prefer not to revisit.

Fireside Chat is a Beacon-exclusive talk show where Critical Role’s co-founders answer questions submitted by Critters through the organization's Discord server. Along with discussing future projects, Ray took the time to answer a question about which storyline she’d like one of her characters to take center stage in during a future live show.

In a recent development, immediately, Ray acknowledged that she felt the tech giant had explored a lot of stories with Vox Machina and the Mighty Nein, and that she’d love to explore new things with Bells Hells or “other stuff,” like one-shots from other eras of Exandria, such as Calamity or Age of Arcanum. But there was one format that Ray shut down right away, despite being one of the most popular live demonstrates in Critical Role history.

According to recent reports, “No more wedding one-shots!” Ray remarked, acknowledging a comment on the Beacon Discord server about her character, Keyleth, getting a wedding. “No! This is going to be a hot take and I’m really sorry, but we had the craziest wedding live show at Radio City Music Hall. I don’t want to top that, man.”.

Ray acknowledged that weddings were a favorite among Critters. “I understand everybody loves weddings, I get it,” she said on the show. “But I don’t want to keep re-treading old territory.”.

Ray isn’t wrong, especially in her comment about revisiting old territory. Just a year ago, Travis Willingham and Laura Bailey reprised their roles as Fjord Stone and Jester Lavorre in “Jester and Fjord's Wedding - Live from Radio City Music Hall” one-shot. Though it still felt very much like a Dungeons & Dragons adventure, with the party fighting off hags and the like, it also featured an actual wedding ceremony. Bailey and Willingham both dressed in wedding outfits, as did the rest of the cast, making it undoubtedly one of the biggest and most elaborate live highlights Critical Role had ever done.

Critical Role also featured the wedding of Percy and Vex in “Dalen's Closet,” a special one-shot rather than a live show. That one also included some dressing up, but unlike the Fjord and Jester one-shot, it was filmed in Critical Role’s studio.

Recent findings suggest that even so, as Ray says, there are only so many one-shots the cast and crew can do. There are plenty of romantic pairings in Exandria we’d love to see celebrated at weddings, such as Imogen and Laudna or Beau and Yasha, but repeating the format could become stale in both gameplay and narrative. How else can you spice up a wedding in a way that feels natural without turning it into a TV soap opera?

Sources indicate that ray’s answer doesn’t rule out another wedding one-shot; opinions can change over time, of course. That mentioned, Critters hoping to hear wedding bells for their favorite characters should wish for something else for now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”].

According to recent reports, it should come as little surprise that David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” focuses on, well, Cliff Booth. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to the filmmaker’s own 2019 Oscar-winning hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” has always been billed as a spinoff following the continuing adventures of his fictitious (yet still iconic) stuntman Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). But Tarantino has always loved building out his own shared and connected universe(s), and fans sure love exploring its outer limits.

“Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and, by extension, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” occupy a unique place in Tarantino’s cinematic world, as they’re both part of his so-called “Realer Than Real World Universe” and his “Movie Movie Universe.” Tarantino didn’t just keep crafting his movies-within-movies world with the hit film — he also introduced real-world (realer than real world?) elements and people (the Manson Family, of course, and all that entails). Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

That bent continues in “Cliff Booth,” which is rife with both out-there elements and very real references (time for that “Hee Haw” resurgence, we guess). But the film also has to follow its own series logic, which means, yes, it’s the Cliff Booth show, but hey, where are our “Hollywood” co-stars Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie)?

[Once again: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”].

Industry observers note that when we first meet Cliff and Rick, the duo are long-time colleagues and best pals. As his stunt double, Cliff is tasked with doing some serious heavy lifting for Hollywood star Rick, which inevitably (?) leads them to off four members of the Manson Family. The raucous and wild violence the duo inflicts on the foursome isn’t just a fun bonding exercise for the pair. It also ensures that the nefarious group can’t go next door to enact the infamous (and very real) Tate murders. Win-win!

The film ends with an invitation for Rick to slide on over to the Tate house for a thank-you drink, presumably putting him in the path of Roman Polanski, Sharon, and all the star power they carry. “Cliff Booth” is set eight years after those events, and while Rick may have enjoyed a career upswing in the interim, his current professional endeavors have taken him far from Hollywood.

In a recent development, while we never see Rick in the film (despite ongoing rumors that DiCaprio might appear for a quick cameo), Cliff mentions him frequently and fondly, including telling potential paramour Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) that their professional entanglements ended when Rick got, ahem, “too fat” for Cliff to believably double him and then moved to Australia to star in the TV series “Dingo Dan.” Further details on the show are slim, but we do know it’s a Western TV show that’s proven quite popular and durable (Aussie Karen seems to like it), and Cliff makes it sound like Rick is enjoying himself. Not too bad.

Industry observers note that by blending his two movie universes with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Tarantino got to both delight in late-’60s Hollywood magic and “save” Sharon Tate, her unborn son, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski, Steven Parent, and Jay Sebring. That sort of revisionist history was the film’s buzziest twist and, as I argued at the time, the most emotional choice Tarantino has ever made in his filmography.

Recent findings suggest that and while we don’t get treated to much more Sharon in “Cliff Booth,” we are granted some, in the form of a Red Apple Cigarettes commercial led by a beaming Margot Robbie, returning to her original role as the doomed actress. (The fake cigarettes are another Tarantino-verse staple, and Rick even appears in his own commercial for them during the end credits of “Hollywood.”).

In the short cameo, Sharon looks healthy and happy, and she’s clearly still enough of a star to warrant her own advertising campaign, built on her smile and her zippy shimmy. As Cliff watches the commercial at the Marina del Rey condo he shares with his dad (Peter Weller), he takes the time to stop, observe, and notably smile at the star. It’s a small grace note, and a very effective one.

It has been revealed that one other star of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” is missing from “Cliff Booth,” though. Just where the heck is Brandy?

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

The geography of Earth in the Marvel Cinematic Universe is mostly similar to our own world, but it does have a few fictional countries thrown in, including Wakanda, Sokovia, and now Latveria. The home nation of Victor von Doom/Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.), Latveria is sandwiched between Romania, Hungary, and Serbia in Marvel's comics, but it's generally just sort of vaguely Eastern European. That means that the role of Doctor Doom in "Avengers: Doomsday" called for a vaguely Eastern European accent.

Sources indicate that based on what we've heard from the film's trailers so far, especially this new international teaser for "Avengers: Doomsday," Downey certainly seems to have delivered on the "vague" part. In this latest promo, Doom challenges a warning that "You shall all kneel before Doom," while also conveniently acting as a bit of a hype man by name-checking some of the massive superhero teams that will appear in the movie. (The Thunderbolts are missing from the list, though, possibly because Doom was confused by their branding).

New international teaser for 'AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY'.

In theaters December 18. pic.twitter.com/wTudC8pKc9.

— Avengers Updates (@AvengersUpdated) November 24, 2026.

According to recent reports, downey's Doom accent has been widely compared to the voice of ancient vampire Nandor the Relentless (Kayvan Novak) in the TV show "What We Do in the Shadows." (Nandor is also from a fictional country, Al Qolnidar.) However, in this particular teaser it's more reminiscent of eccentric German filmmaker Werner Herzog. Even Downey himself has said that he struggled to settle on an accent.

Recent findings suggest that "Part of me didn't want to go Eastern European," Robert Downey Jr. explained, regarding Doctor Doom's accent, in an interview with Empire. "I had written this manifesto speech that [Doom] makes, and I laid down this voice note of him addressing his people, and I started to find it there.".

In a recent development, downey already appeared in 10 Marvel Cinematic Universe movies as Tony Stark, aka Iron Man, so Doom presented a fresh challenge for him: "I don't want to say Tony's like rolling off a log, but I know that swing pattern." Comparatively, the process of figuring out Doom, from superficialities like his accent to his deeper motivations, was "painstaking." The fact that the character spends most of his time — possibly the entire movie, if you believe Downey's co-star Chris Evans — wearing a full face mask presented another challenge. "Honestly, a lot of it was just the eyes," Downey told Empire, adding, "I ain't gonna lie to you. A lot of this we were just trying to figure it out ... It was a bit of an exploration.".

Recent findings suggest that the question of whether or not Doom will take his mask off is a major one, as Downey's face is pretty recognizable within the world of the MCU. For now, though, much about Doom is still shrouded in mystery. 📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (414 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mega Evolution returned to the Pokémon Trading Card Game with the launch of the Mega Evolution series in 2025.
  • Recent findings suggest that given how rare these cards are, most collectors lucky enough to find them quickly sent them to PSA for grading.
  • According to recent reports, in an official blog post, PSA explains that some English-language Mega Hyper Rare Pokémon cards are defective, and therefore, none can be accurately graded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mega Evolution returned to the Pokémon Trading Card Game with the launch of the Mega Evolution series in 2025. In this expansion, collectors can find extremely rare Mega Evolution Pokémon EX cards known as Mega Hyper Rare cards in English and Mega Ultra Rare cards in Japanese. These holographic secret cards show alternative artwork of Pokémon's Mega Evolutions on a beautiful gold-etched display.

Recent findings suggest that given how rare these cards are, most collectors lucky enough to find them quickly sent them to PSA for grading. Unfortunately, in many cases, this will no longer be possible. On Nov. 25, 2026, the PSA declared that it has stopped grading English-language Mega Hyper Rare Pokémon cards effective immediately.

According to recent reports, in an official blog post, PSA explains that some English-language Mega Hyper Rare Pokémon cards are defective, and therefore, none can be accurately graded. Card grading experts "identified a manufacturing matter that can cause the gold foil on the front of these cards to deteriorate over time, leaving visible patches or fading." While the severity of the defect varies from card to card, it's impossible to determine whether a card will eventually be affected by it and deteriorate. The issue can arise even if the card is properly stored and encapsulated.

It has been revealed that "A card can begin deteriorating after it’s graded, even with no visible signs at first, so we can’t assign a grade that will reliably hold. Continuing to grade these cards wouldn’t meet the standard of accuracy and consistency that collectors rely on us for.".

Recent findings suggest that grades already assigned to English-language Mega Hyper Rare cards by PSA will not be revoked and can be submitted for Review and Reholder service, allowing collectors to reevaluate their condition. Cards in transit or submitted for grading will be returned ungraded, and PSA will waive the grading service fee as compensation.

On the bright side, PSA states that Japanese-language Mega Ultra Rare Pokémon cards do not appear to be defective, as they were printed at a facility that uses different techniques, and can be submitted for grading for the time being.

It is right now unknown how this will affect card prices. It could go either way. The price of defective cards might rise before the manufacturing error is fixed, or it could fall sharply, as collectors begin their search for a pristine Japanese MUR card or look for an already graded English-language card instead.

Forget the MCU. Real ones know that Quentin Tarantino has been building his own cinematic universe for years. For instance: while this is never officially stated by anyone on screen, Michael Madsen's character from "Reservoir Dogs" is supposed to be the brother of John Travolta's character from "Pulp Fiction" (there was even a plan for a crossover movie, but it never happened). Beyond character connections, Tarantino also likes to drop his own fictional products into his films, and "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps this trend going.

Tarantino didn't direct "Cliff Booth" — he handed those duties over to David Fincher. But Tarantino still wrote the script, and Fincher keeps the Easter eggs intact. The biggest example: Significant Kahuna Burger. Early in the film, we see Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth pick up some food at Big Kahuna Burger to bring home to his dad, Gus (Peter Weller). Tarantino fans will, of course, recognize that burger joint: it was prominently mentioned in "Pulp Fiction," and we see Samuel L. Jackson's character Jules take a big bite of a burger while intimidating some crooks who are about to meet a violent end.

But wait, there's more! Another Tarantino product that reveals up in "The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" are the famous Red Apple Cigarettes. Red Apples have been mentioned in virtually every Tarantino film, and they were even a part of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the film that "Cliff Booth" serves as a sequel to.

In a recent development, in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton filmed a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes (believe it or not, kids, there used to be commercials for cigarettes on TV). "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps the tradition alive while also giving us a nice little callback. During one scene, we see Cliff watching a upcoming Red Apple commercial on TV. And who is starring in that commercial? None other than Sharon Tate, played by Margot Robbie in a cameo.

In a recent development, "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" ended by literally changing history, and allowing Sharon Tate and her friends to completely avoid their tragic murders at the hands of the Manson family. "Cliff Booth" confirms that since Sharon is still alive in 1977, when the film is set, she's still out there acting, too.

  • Deschanel had met Kaufman years earlier when Deschanel was a film student at USC, and Kaufman was a young director working on the Western “The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid.” “A couple friends and I put on these rock indicates at Shrine Auditorium, and he came to a couple of those,” Deschanel told IndieWire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“The Right Stuff” was released 43 years ago, but its spectacular aerial and outer space sequences have lost none of their power. Director Philip Kaufman’s adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s book, which traced the history of the test pilots who became the first astronauts, features immersive set pieces that are still as convincing as ever, in spite of decades of technological advancements since it was made. To revisit it via Criterion‘s latest 4K UHD physical media release is to experience one of the most groundbreaking and enduring films of all time.

The new Criterion transfer was supervised by cinematographer Caleb Deschanel, who was still relatively early in his career when Kaufman tapped him to shoot “The Right Stuff.” Deschanel didn’t have many feature credits, but the ones he did have were impressive: his early work included the stunning imagery of “The Black Stallion” and two Hal Ashby movies, “Being There” and the Rolling Stones concert film “Let’s Spend the Night Together.” He would earn the first of his six Academy Award nominations for “The Right Stuff.” Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing for Thanksgiving 2026?

Deschanel had met Kaufman years earlier when Deschanel was a film student at USC, and Kaufman was a young director working on the Western “The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid.” “A couple friends and I put on these rock indicates at Shrine Auditorium, and he came to a couple of those,” Deschanel told IndieWire. Deschanel visited the set of “Minnesota” and stayed in touch with Kaufman, who called him around 10 years later with the offer to shoot “The Right Stuff.”.

“It was a dream come true,” Deschanel remarked, noting that he had always been an aviation buff who loved going to air reveals with his father. He also remembered that Kaufman wasn’t the only person on “The Right Stuff” who he had met years earlier. “Years before we had moved into our first house and needed some painting done, and we had a friend who was teaching in the Cal Arts theater department. He said, ‘I have this actor who’s really great who paints houses in the summer.'”.

According to recent reports, deschanel hired the young actor and got to know him a little bit, and five years later was having lunch with his wife Mary Jo and Kaufman when Kaufman demonstrated them a picture of the actor he had chosen to play John Glenn. “I mentioned, ‘We know him. That’s Ed Harris. He painted our house,'” Deschanel said. “Then, coincidentally, the woman who was supposed to play Annie Glenn dropped out of and Phil cast my wife, so they ended up playing husband and wife in the movie.”.

Sources indicate that one of the great technical challenges of “The Right Stuff” was integrating archival footage of the space race with the fresh material being shot — one of the reasons the movie was shot in a 1.85:1 aspect ratio instead of a wider Panavision format as one might have expected for such an epic film. “We were using actual footage of NASA’s rocket debuts and things like that, and they were filming in the old-fashioned 4:3 format using the full frame of a 35mm camera,” Deschanel said. “Converting that to widescreen was really impossible.”.

Working in close collaboration with visual effects supervisor Gary Gutierrez (who provides a fascinating look at the film’s miniature and rear-projection work on the Criterion disc), Deschanel solved the numerous logistical problems that came with trying to make it look as though the actors were hurtling through the air at the speed of sound and beyond. Even when Gutierrez thought he had solutions that would work, they often had to be tweaked to accommodate Kaufman’s desire to make everything feel as realistic and immersive as possible.

Sources indicate that early attempts to use a motion-control system for the effects, for example, were discarded because the camera movement was too smooth for Kaufman’s purposes. “Phil wanted it to have some energy to it,” Deschanel mentioned. “That changed the whole methodology.” Whenever rockets were taking off or various crafts were flying, Deschanel made sure to add some shake to the camera. “I actually gave my camera operator, Craig Denault, a black eye at one point because I was hitting the camera so hard.”.

In addition to the expected challenges, there were plenty of unexpected ones as well — like the fact that Sam Shepard, who played ace pilot Chuck Yeager, wouldn’t fly. “The only time he ever went up in an airplane was when Yeager took him for a flight,” Deschanel remarked. “Other than that, whenever we had a mockup of an X-1 or the F-104 or anything like that, he’d make me get in and show him how it was going to twist and turn before he would get into it.” For Yeager’s scenes and many of the others, rear projection was used — meaning Deschanel had to photograph what was seen outside the pilots’ and astronauts’ windows long before the actors’ material was actually shot.

According to recent reports, “There was a lot of complexity to all those things,” Deschanel mentioned. “But it gave it a real energy and sense of being there. And that’s what you try to discover as you’re filming any film: what is that visual metaphor that really makes you believe you’re having the same experience the characters are having?” Creating that sense of authenticity required some unorthodox approaches, as when Deschanel had a Learjet pilot take the nose cone off of his plane and replace it with a clear dome.

Industry observers note that “We put a camera in there with a 15mm lens, and then we were able to go up above 50,000 feet,” Deschanel said. “At that level, it’s so dark, it’s almost like you’re in outer space. Anything you could think of to find the reality of the movie, we employed.” Deschanel’s perfectionism became the stuff of legend over the years, with some people who worked on “The Right Stuff” claiming he insisted on shooting only at sunrise or sunset to get the most beautiful possible images — a myth Deschanel is quick to dispel.

Sources indicate that “The fact is we shot all day long and had really long days,” Deschanel remarked. “There was one point where, just to finish up at Edwards Air Force Base, I was on for 24 hours and changed the crew in the middle. So I had a whole new crew for the second half of that long day.” That said, Deschanel acknowledges that the film’s justly famous exteriors were crucial to him, in part for what they represented.

“The iconic moment is when Yeager is on horseback, and he rides up and sees the X-1,” Deschanel said. “It’s like ‘The Professionals’ or ‘The Wild Bunch,’ these movies about the end of the West as new technology takes over. To me, there’s this wonderful representation of the end of an era when Yeager comes across this fighter jet. Then, of course, he flies it and breaks the sound barrier. So it’s this wonderful juxtaposition of key moments in human history, where one person does something that further advances flight to the point that makes it possible for the next generation to go into outer space. I always miss that I never got to make a Western, but in a way, ‘The Right Stuff’ is a Western.”.

“The Right Stuff” special edition 4K UHD release is now available from Criterion.

He would have focused on a pair of beloved characters, specifically the best droids in the "Star Wars" property.

On a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Fincher revealed that he had a conversation with former Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy about taking th studio public before Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012. But what would Fincher have done with "Star Wars" had that panned out? Perhaps not what you'd expect.

It has been revealed that his interest lay with C-3PO and R2-D2, primarily. Not Luke Skywalker. Not Princess Leia. A protocol droid and his astromech companion. And while Fincher admitted he didn't have a full pitch, he did have a rough idea. Here's what he had to say:.

"I noted, 'The thing that has always interested me about — certainly from the first movie — was the relationship between [C-]3PO and R2[-D2]. That they were essentially slaves who would bear witness to the folly of man. I always thought that, them being captured by Jawas, and then sold off and being on the periphery and witnessing the Skywalker Saga, was such a crucial element to it. [...] There was a kind of moral judgment. It was fairly obvious even from 3PO [...] he had a kind of understanding as to what the Empire meant, how evil they were.".

"He was kind of trying to decide whether or not he wanted to invest in having a relationship with Luke Skywalker when he's getting his oil bath [in 'A New Hope'], and they're talking," Fincher added.

"Even from ['The Empire Strikes Back'], when 3PO is turned back on, and he recounts for you what he sees with the stormtroopers already being in [...] Bespin," David FIncher continued. "Whenever they used the robots for that, I was always really excited. I always thought that was kind of interesting, that you have to go through the recorder, like the court reporter, to find out what it is that happened.".

Industry observers note that notably, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels is the only actor to appear in all nine main "Star Wars" movies, while Kenny Baker portrayed R2-D2 in the original trilogy. These are characters who certainly have earned time in the spotlight, but using them as the crux of a new era for the franchise? That's a strange idea.

Be that as it may, Fincher and Kathleen Kennedy were interested in seeing if they could make something happen. Fincher, however, revealed that Disney's purchase of Lucasfilm (a deal that encompassed $4 billion in cash and stocks) nixed those plans. As the filmmaker recalled:.

Sources indicate that "I noted to [Kennedy], I kind of pitched her this idea, I said, 'Let's take this thing to Wall Street and let the market decide.' And I think it was a month later or something, she said, 'Bad news. Apparently there's a $7 billion offer on the table,' and I said, 'We're not going to beat that.'".

George Lucas later opened up about selling Lucafilm to Disney, describing it as "very, very painful." Of course, it proved to be enormously beneficial for Disney, financially speaking. Fincher, meanwhile, has gone on to continue enjoying a very fruitful career outside the confines of a galaxy far, far away.

Tech Report: Blade Runner 2099 Revives A Major Element From Philip K. Dick's Original Novel

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K.
  • Industry observers note that to be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen.
  • Industry observers note that this idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," didn't exactly make it to the substantial screen fully intact. As influential and unique as it is, Dick's work proved too unwieldy for filmmakers to adapt wholesale. Instead, Hollywood took Dick's themes and concepts and heavily rewrote his stories for the screen. That trend began with "Blade Runner," as original screenwriter Hampton Fancher took the neo-noir concept from Dick's trippy, weird 1968 novel of a human hunting down illegal androids and pretty much discarded the rest. The relationship between "Androids" and "Blade Runner" can be succinctly summed up by the fact that Fancher and director Ridley Scott didn't use Dick's title for the film, eventually going so far as to borrow the title from a completely different novel by William S. Burroughs.

Industry observers note that to be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen. Yet numerous other plot elements and characters were either altered or omitted altogether. One element in "Androids" which is very important to Dick's worldbuilding is the concept of Mercerism, a religion in which devotees share a looping, pre-programmed experience via a virtual reality machine called an empathy box.

Industry observers note that this idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series. The use of Mercerism in the Prime Video show is a great example of showrunner Silka Luisa and her writers knowing Dick and "Blade Runner" well. In fact, the inclusion of a missing element of Dick's novel in a "Blade Runner" sequel is a bit of a franchise tradition.

Recent findings suggest that in "Blade Runner 2099," it initially seems that Silka Luisa and manufacturer have included Mercerism as a little Easter egg, as a couple of animated billboards in Los Angeles advertise it. Yet this isn't a winking reference to Philip K. Dick's novel, but is instead foreshadowing. In Episode 6, entitled "Kill the Killers," Cora (Hunter Schafer) and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) travel to a hideaway where Cora and her brother grew up. It turns out this hideaway is a defunct Mercer Monastery, a place where those who worship the man could come to and use an empathy box or interact with automated priest-like programs (shades of George Lucas' "THX 1138" there).

Mercerism, as detailed in Dick's "Androids," is a religion based around the idea of increasing empathy, since the future of the novel has become so dystopian and isolating that people need to be reminded to have empathy for others (sound familiar?). This is done through the empathy box, which allows consumers to experience a moment from the life of Wilbur Mercer, apparently some kind of martyr. In the box, Mercer endlessly climbs up a hill while being pelted with rocks, and the "empathy" the user experiences is holding onto sensors which deliver increasingly harsher shocks, sometimes resulting in death.

Recent findings suggest that the idea was first introduced by Dick in a short story in 1964 entitled "The Little Black Box," and then re-used in "Androids." The ironic twist in "Androids" is that Mercerism is revealed to be a total sham, with the video loop having been shot on a soundstage with an actor. Though this isn't addressed in "2099," the obvious decline in Mercerites and decay of the monastery implies that the religion isn't as popular as it once was.

Recent findings suggest that even though Mercerism didn't make it into a previous iteration of "Blade Runner," the themes behind it are so integral to the story of "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and its world that its inclusion feels natural. "Blade Runner 2099" smoothly weaves it into its storyline, using it as an allegory for its doomed principal characters as well as its apocalyptic vision of Earth in general. It's used in the show in much the same way Dick uses it in "Androids," as a satiric commentary on how what was initially intended as an aspirational endeavor has devolved into something more pathetic than never believing in it in the first place.

Ironically, Mercerism is not the first element in "Androids" that was left out of "Blade Runner" but made a return appearance in a sequel story to Ridley Scott's film. In "Androids," the character of John R. Isidore (or J.R. Isidore) was reconceived and rewritten as J.F. Sebastian for "Blade Runner," and he was killed during the events of the film. However, when Dick's friend K.W. Jeter wrote the 1995 novel "Blade Runner 2: The Edge of Human," Jeter brought J.R. Isidore back into the story. It's not entirely clear if Jeter intends his Isidore to be the literal same character, or if he's "borrowing" the character in the same manner as Dick borrowed Mercerism from his short story for "Androids." Either way, it established a neat little tradition for the franchise, in which anything or anyone could come back, and perhaps come back different. For a series infamous for characters not ever fully knowing their true identity and heritage, the tradition feels rather poignant.

"Blade Runner 2099" is now streaming on Prime Video.

10 Years Later, Netflix's $120 Million Flop Deserves a Season 2

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in 2016, Netflix was riding high.
  • According to recent reports, this Turkey Day, as Polygon celebrates our favorite failures and flops from the world of entertainment, it's time to resurrect a Netflix original that earned (mostly) rave reviews but got canceled after just one season for what, in hindsight, feels like an easily avoidable reason.
  • Created by Baz Luhrmann (Moulin Rouge, The Great Gatsby, Romeo + Juliet) and playwright Stephen Adly Guirgis, The Get Down traces the origin story of hip-hop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 2016, Netflix was riding high. The shift to original programming, which had kicked off three years earlier with House of Cards, was now proving to be an undeniable success. That year marked the return of hit shows like Daredevil, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt, BoJack Horseman, and Orange is the New Black, along with the debut of brand-defining series Stranger Things and The Crown. All of these shows have remained in the cultural zeitgeist, but arguably the best original series released on Netflix in 2016 has all but disappeared from the conversation.

According to recent reports, this Turkey Day, as Polygon celebrates our favorite failures and flops from the world of entertainment, it's time to resurrect a Netflix original that earned (mostly) rave reviews but got canceled after just one season for what, in hindsight, feels like an easily avoidable reason. Not only is The Get Down an overlooked masterpiece, but 10 years later, it's due for a revival.

Created by Baz Luhrmann (Moulin Rouge, The Great Gatsby, Romeo + Juliet) and playwright Stephen Adly Guirgis, The Get Down traces the origin story of hip-hop. Deep within the Bronx, MCs hype local crowds with rhythmic lyricism performed over percussive instrumental breaks pulled by pioneering DJs from funk, soul, and disco records. The series centers on one such MC, Zeke "Books" Figuero (Justice Smith), and his DJ, Curtis "Shaolin Fantastic" Caldwell (Shameik Moore), as they stumble into a newly introduced art form.

It has been revealed that while much of the story follows these two young Black men as they hustle and struggle to succeed, The Get Down's scope is even grander. It's the story of Latest York City in the 1970s and everything that entails, from corrupt politicians and gangsters to the rising punk music scene in Manhattan. Disco defines the series almost as much as hip-hop, with female protagonist Mylene Cruz (Herizen F. Guardiola) representing the power of the then-dominant genre as a beautiful woman with an incredible voice who's stuck singing in church when she wants to be a radio star.

Industry observers note that the absolutely stacked cast also includes Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as gangster disco prince Clarence "Cadillac" Caldwell, Jimmy Smits as a local political boss, Giancarlo Esposito as Mylene's pastor father, Mamoudou Athie as real-life DJ legend Grandmaster Flash, and Daveed Diggs as adult Ezekiel narrating the story (with hip-hop icon Nas providing his dubbed-in rapping voice). It's an all-star team-up firing on all cylinders.

In a recent development, the Get Down has all the usual flourishes of a Luhrmann production. It's a beautifully realized world that glitters in the neon lights of Upcoming York without attempting to hide the crime and decay that defined the city in the 1970s. Telling a story about hip-hop and disco also allows Luhrmann to fill the show with elevated musical moments that are on par with the best scenes from Moulin Rouge, while also feeling far more grounded. This isn't a musical in the sense that characters don't spontaneously break into song to move the plot forward or express their emotions, but it still manages to achieve a similarly staggering effect each time a record spins and an MC picks up the mic.

Recent findings suggest that it's also deeply reverent toward the history of hip-hop. Music icons Nas, Grandmaster Flash, and Kurtis Blow organized a hip-hop boot camp to teach the young cast about the art form. In an interview with Mother Jones, Grandmaster Flash praised the series for demystifying the earliest origins of the genre he helped create.

"Hip-hop has always been chronologically misunderstood," he said. "Too many times, people are hearing the story from the second floor. Nobody’s heard the story from the basement. If hip-hop was a cake, all I can tell you is the eggs, the flour, the sugar, the vanilla — the ingredient years. This is what Baz wanted to put on film.".

Meanwhile, Nas, who arrived in the '90s and redefined rap music with his vibrant descriptions of life in the Brooklyn projects, conveyed through naturalistic lyrical poetry, wrote every single bar delivered by Ezekiel on the show.

"I am Ezekiel," he told Rolling Stone. "Ezekiel is older than me, but I am that.".

In a recent development, in other words, The Get Down wasn't just Luhrmann's retelling of a famous story. It was a deeply researched, loving tribute to the creation of hip-hop, told by the people who defined the genre from the very start.

The Get Down dropped six episodes on Netflix in August 2016, with another five released in April 2017 to complete the first season. The second batch picks up a year later in the story as well, with Mylene's singing career taking off while Ezekiel struggles to keep up, weighed down by the world he grew up in.

The show was canceled soon afterward for a variety of reasons, including its astronomical cost. In an article breaking down the rise and fall of The Get Down, IndieWire called it "the best $120 million Netflix has ever spent.".

Ultimately, the show's downfall reportedly traces back to Luhrmann. While the director took a hands-on approach in crafting season 1 (even directing the pilot episode himself), he decided to take a step back with season 2 to return to film and make Elvis. This didn't mean the show had to stop, though. In a sense, that approach had pretty much defined the entire series from day one.

According to recent reports, “Because I come from community storytelling, you have to get the community’s trust,” Luhrmann told IndieWire. “So I started to reach out to the people whose story it was, because it’s not my story. I feel like I just curated that story.”.

But Netflix balked, and The Get Down came to a disappointingly early end. In a sense, it was a sign of things to come. In the years since, the streamer has developed an unfortunate reputation for canceling great reveals too early and for relying on substantial-name talent over good storytelling and original ideas (although The Get Down had plenty of both).

Recent findings suggest that A decade after its demise, the chances of a revival seem slim. There isn't exactly a devoted fanbase crying out for more, and Luhrmann is already busy working on his next movie. Then again, it's not totally impossible either. After all, The Get Down's core duo has only gotten more famous in the years since, with Shameik Moore voicing Miles Morales in the Spider-Verse movies and Justice Smith starring in everything from Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves to Now You See Me: Now You Don't. Maybe that's enough to entice some Netflix executive.

Recent findings suggest that A follow-up could reunite Smith and Moore (and the rest of the cast) and pick up their story a decade later. The late '80s was a golden age for hip-hop, with artists like Eric B. & Rakim, Major Daddy Kane, LL Cool J, Public Enemy, and N.W.A dominating the airwaves on both sides of the country. A fresh season of The Get Down could explore what happens when an art form born out of the Bronx projects goes mainstream — and how that kind of explosive success can often leave the original creators behind.

In a recent development, is it a long shot​​​​​​​? Of course, but either way, The Get Down remains a shining example of what's starting to feel like the long-gone golden age of Netflix programming. So why not give it a spin? And maybe if enough people do, we'll finally get a season 2.

However, Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower offers a totally different side of the star’s screen persona.

A three-part docudrama that focuses on the history of the Mayflower voyage, Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower is a Fox Nation series that focuses on the events of the First Thanksgiving. Beginning with the Pilgrims’ journey to America and extending its focus to the first contact between the Wampanoag people and English invaders, the log line of the series promises that Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower will then focus on the devastating conflict that followed.

According to Deadline, Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower’s creative team spoke to Plimoth Patuxet Museum’s resident historians as well as consulting Nathaniel Philbrick, the author of Mayflower: A Story of Courage, Community, and War. The history of Thanksgiving has often been a thorny topic on television, with one of Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s most infamously misjudged episodes attempting to address the holiday’s history and falling flat in the process.

According to recent reports, it isn’t easy to make such a familiar story feel fresh, especially when a radically different perspective on the history of the era is likely to upset the expectations of some viewers. This can leave TV creators in a tough double bind, where the traditional narrative is overly well-worn, but a new one could prove too challenging for audiences who expect a specific version of history.

It has been revealed that fortunately, Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower boasts a secret weapon in this regard. The show’s celebrity narrator elevates its potential, since Thornton’s Southern drawl would be engaging even if he were reading a phone book aloud. Earlier historical docudramas like the 2026 hit World War II with Tom Hanks and Pompeii: Out of Time with Tom Hiddleston took the same approach.

Sources indicate that by borrowing the star of one of TV’s hottest TV highlights, Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower can reinvent a tired chapter in US history for a upcoming generation of viewers. Landman fans now have the perfect Thanksgiving binge thanks to the show’s timely arrival, while anyone unfamiliar with the history of the holiday has an ideal primer.

While Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower is only a three-part docudrama, this length does mean that the Fox Nation show is the ideal weekend binge over the holiday season. As such, Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower couldn’t be arriving at a more fortuitous time for viewers.

  • There's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, "Avatar" fans can thank Eywa, because more sequels are indeed coming. As reported by Collider, Disney's upcoming film release slate includes "Avatar 4" (dated for December 21, 2029) and "Avatar 5" (dated for December 19, 2031). These dates aren't necessarily etched in stone; during the 2010s, the release date for "Avatar: The Way of Water" got pushed back so much that many convinced themselves the movie was never coming out. You simply can't rush the quality that director James Cameron demands of the "Avatar" films. But it's a sign Disney wants the movies out sooner than later.

In a recent development, was the future of a billion dollar franchise like "Avatar" ever in doubt? Keep in mind, the third movie, 2025's "Avatar: Fire and Ash," was the lowest grossing movie in the series. It still grossed just under $1.5 billion, but that's a notably diminished return next to "The Way of Water," which pulled $2.3 billion internationally. "Fire and Ash" was also, like its predecessors, one of the most expensive movies ever made.

There's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects. Cameron is currently working on "Ghosts of Hiroshima," based on the non-fiction book by author Charles Pellegrino, and he's likewise attached to an adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's dark fantasy book "The Devils.".

Cameron, who is 72 years old, is in the stage of his life where he has to balance the films he wants to make against the time he has left, and he knows it. As he told the Empire Film podcast back in May 2026, he wants to make the fourth and fifth "Avatar" films in less time, and for less money, than it took to make "The Way of Water" and "Fire and Ash.".

James Cameron told People in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will feature a six-year time jump. Parts of the film were even shot concurrently with "Fire and Ash" to capture the series' younger actors, like Jack Champion (Spider) and Trinity Bliss (Tuktirey), while they still pass as kids.

The "Avatar" films have strong environmentalist themes; humanity wants to colonize Pandora because, by the 22nd century, Earth is polluted, overpopulated, and seemingly dying. We've only seen small glimpses of that in the previous films. Producer Jon Landau told Syfy back in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will change that:.

It has been revealed that "There's over-population and a depletion of our natural resources that make life harder. But we don't want to paint a bleak picture for where our world is going. The films are also about the idea of that we can change course.".

What about lingering threads on Pandora? "Fire and Ash" ended with the recombinant Colonel Miles Quaritch (Stephen Lang) seemingly plummeting to his death. But one of the most essential rules of fiction is if you don't see a dead body, and sometimes even if you do, don't treat mortal peril as confirmed death.

According to recent reports, quaritch already beat death once, and it feels like he still hasn't quite completed his story yet. Even if Lang/Quaritch does sit "Avatar 4" out, "Fire and Ash" ended with his accomplice Varang (Oona Chaplin) still at large. Varang was easily the breakout character of "Fire and Ash," and I'd be shocked if we don't see her return to attack the Sully family again in movie number four.

"Avatar 4" is right now scheduled for theatrical release on December 21, 2029.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s been four years since the cult hit “Hundreds of Beavers” first debuted and still two years since it started really gaining traction with wider audiences in 2024. But if it feels like the black and white, silent, slapstick indie comedy still hasn’t left the cultural conversation, that’s because in all that time it has continued to quietly play in theaters and attract audiences both loyal and fresh alike.

According to recent reports, technically, “Hundreds of Beavers” has never left theaters. It continues to play individual screenings in a city or two every weekend. Now, though, “Hundreds of Beavers” is set to return to theaters for what is its biggest theatrical expansions to date. The film will kick off its third annual Northwoods Christmas, which will feature 130 screenings across 85 cities, with more to likely be added in the coming weeks. It came about after another fan campaign pushed for the film to come to some markets it hadn’t previously thought about or targeted such as Indianapolis and Charlottesville, and it will now play in everything from concert venues to microcinemas. Related Stories Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’ Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

According to recent reports, the re-releases have become a holiday tradition for “Hundreds of Beavers,” which for all its wintery setting and its main character dressed like Santa, is being positioned as a latest Christmas movie. The first time “Hundreds of Beavers” was re-released at Christmas 2024, which was shortly after the Blu-ray for the film became available, it brought in $118K at the box office in a month, and the producers continued the tradition in 2025.

“There’s room for a Christmas tradition with the energy of a ‘Rocky Horror’ screening,” remarked producer Kurt Ravenwood. “You can watch ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ and ‘White Christmas’ all you want, but for getting together with friends and family to laugh about the miserable winter ahead, ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ has them all beat.”.

Each of the screenings will be preceded by a short film featuring “Bing Crosbeaver,” which they did last year, but this will be a new short with a new twist in which another character named “Conspirabeaver” will be joined by a “sinister foe,” per the release. Some of the in-person beavers in costume will be present at the screenings, and fans will also get a promotional poster for the movie. The “Beavers” team recently released a few parody posters ripping off the recent releases of “You Can See Everything,” “Digger,” and “The Devils.”.

To date, “Hundreds of Beavers” has made $940,092 at the domestic box office, including another $618,014 internationally to bring its worldwide total to above $1.5 million. It’s done all this via first producing the film for just $150,000 and spending little more than $70,000 on ads, publicity, and its many roadshow screenings. It’s also been released entirely independently, starting with a run in the Midwest where the film is set before it started expanding to the coasts.

It has been revealed that incredibly, more than 70 percent of the film’s U.S. box office has come after “Hundreds of Beavers” began streaming way back on April 15, 2024, and it has even sold more than 20,000 Blu-Rays worldwide. It’s a rare, truly indie success story even in a day and age when many movies have pursued self-distribution strategies.

According to recent reports, for those who haven’t had the pleasure of seeing “Hundreds of Beavers” in theaters yet, the film is about a drunken applejack salesman who loses everything and has to survive the winter by becoming North America’s greatest fur trapper. It sees the trapper wrestling and fighting with dozens of beavers and other forest animals all wearing mascot suits, with the stark black and white cinematography and creative physical stunts embracing a zany video game logic and absurd silent comedy slapstick gags.

The film is directed by Mike Cheslik and was written by Cheslik and star Ryland Tews, with the film also starring Olivia Graves, Wes Tank, Doug Mancheski, and Luis Rico.

Industry News: Avengers: Secret Wars Setting Confirmed By Marvel, Spoiling Doomsday

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines.
  • We've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014.
  • The Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines. As it stands, "Doomsday" has a real shot at the biggest box office opening weekend ever, which would bode very well for the second part of Joe and Anthony Russo's upcoming duology, "Avengers: Secret Wars." That sequel is due out on December 17, 2027, and if "Doomsday" does what "Infinity War" did back in 2018, it should have a grand old time at the box office. That is, if Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige doesn't spoil things before then.

We've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014. That arc serves as a prelude to Hickman's 2015 "Secret Wars" storyline, and together these two runs see the Marvel universe collapse due to "incursions," after which Victor von Doom uses fragments of the shattered multiverse to create a newly introduced planet named Battleworld. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, Feige basically confirmed that this is the setting for the MCU's version of "Secret Wars," basically spoiling "Doomsday" by strongly hinting how that film ends and where the next one begins.

The Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made. Look at the comics. The characters and the settings and the worlds within this singular planet where our movie 'Secret Wars' takes place is the imagination gone wild, which is what's exciting about it." So there you have it. Most fans expected to see Battleworld in "Secret Wars," but now it's as close to official as you can get.

The first "Secret Wars" comic book arc arrived in 1984, with writer Jim Shooter and artists Mike Zeck and Bob Layton delivering a story in which the cosmic entity known as The Beyonder forced various Marvel characters to fight to the death on the planet Battleworld. It seems Marvel Studios will draw from this original run for some aspects of "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars." But for the most part, Jonathan Hickman's 2015 run serves as the basis for the two movies.

This second "Secret Wars" arc, illustrated by artist Esad Ribić with cover designs by Alex Ross, and the run that preceded it, "Time Runs Out," are the essential inspiration for "Doomsday" and its sequel. Feige told Entertainment Weekly that "Doomsday" is basically the MCU's version of "Time Runs Out," while the filmmakers described "Secret Wars" as "a little bit of both" that storyline and Hickman's "Secret Wars.".

Recent findings suggest that asked to comment further, Feige mentioned, "If you wanted spoilers for 'The Odyssey,' you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for 'Doomsday' and 'Secret Wars,' you can go look at the comics," adding, "It is very much the same thing that we're doing." Clearly, then, Hickman's work is integral to the two upcoming MCU releases, with Feige going on to say that "Secret Wars" is "very much" the "culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event." With that in mind, you can bet the "Doomsday" sequel will play out pretty much entirely on the MCU's version of Battleworld, with the surviving heroes from "Doomsday" taking the fight to its god emperor, Doom, in an attempt to overthrow his regime and restore the multiverse. Whether "Secret Wars" will include Marvel's infamous Spider-Man bathroom scene, however, remains unconfirmed.

According to recent reports, none of Kevin Feige's latest revelations should come as a big shock to Marvel fans who've known Marvel Studios has been drawing from Jonathan Hickman's "Secret Wars" run. But this is the closest Feige has come to officially confirming Battleworld as the setting for "Avengers: Secret Wars." The Marvel Studios head didn't use the name "Battleworld," but his comments about a "singular planet" were in response to a question about it.

Otherwise, Feige characterized "Avengers: Doomsday" as "a culmination of what's come before," and "Secret Wars" as "a launching pad for [Marvel Studios'] films in 2028 — the 20th anniversary of the MCU." Clearly, then, whatever happens at the end of "Secret Wars" will set the stage for new characters, timelines, and storylines that will reshape the way the MCU looks going forward.

We know that Marvel Studios is preparing its Jake Schrier-directed X-Men movie, which is set to debut in the wake of "Secret Wars." First, though, Marvel is reworking its cinematic universe with "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars." According to co-director Joe Russo, this simply had to be done with two movies due to it being "such a major storyline." He continued: "Doom as a character needs a lot of space, especially when Robert Downey is playing him. So the scale of the story, the emotional scale of the story is so large that it really needed to be a two-parter.".

Industry observers note that whether the second part of that two-parter will actually debut on December 17, 2027, however, remains unclear. Production on "Secret Wars" has been moved to 2027, suggesting a delay might be imminent. For now, we'll have to wait and see how things play out. But regardless of when the movie actually arrives, prepare yourselves for a major screen visit to Battleworld.

Industry News: How Blade Runner 2099 Took Inspiration From Denis Villeneuve's Legacy Sequel [Exclusive]

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it's impossible enough to have to live in the shadow of an unabashed classic of cinema, so just imagine dealing with two of them.
  • For showrunner Silka Luisa, this could've required one of two different approaches: stay suffocatingly faithful to the look and feel and tone of the two films or purposefully set off in the opposite direction.
  • "I knew we were definitely going to have an opportunity to lay our own track, because — it's right in the title, the fact that you're so many years past 2049, it gives you enough space to really carve out your own identity.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it's impossible enough to have to live in the shadow of an unabashed classic of cinema, so just imagine dealing with two of them. There aren't many who would have a bad word to say about Ridley Scott's original "Blade Runner (well, except for those unfortunate critics who dismissed it upon release), but Denis Villeneuve's highly-acclaimed sequel "Blade Runner 2049" ain't too shabby, either. Now, Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" series has the added responsibility of picking up the story where its beloved predecessors left off ... along with all the pressure that comes with that.

For showrunner Silka Luisa, this could've required one of two different approaches: stay suffocatingly faithful to the look and feel and tone of the two films or purposefully set off in the opposite direction. Well, in this case, how about a secret third option instead? During a recent press junket for "Blade Runner 2099," I spoke with Luisa over Zoom about where this show fits in next to its movie kin and how it finds its own niche amid a much wider world:.

"I knew we were definitely going to have an opportunity to lay our own track, because — it's right in the title, the fact that you're so many years past 2049, it gives you enough space to really carve out your own identity.".

According to recent reports, impressively, Luisa looked to Villeneuve's 2017 movie to figure out the ideal way to do just that. "What was so fantastic about what Denis did with '2049' was, he didn't just rehash what Ridley had done," the showrunner told me. "He really created his own take on 'Blade Runner' that is very much his aesthetic. But it still felt like an evolution of Ridley's conversation." In effect, the key was to thread that very tricky needle for "2099.".

When it comes to the recent trend of legacy sequels that have dominated the last decade or so of franchise filmmaking, it can certainly feel like we can count the worthwhile ones on just one or two hands. Fortunately, for Silka Luisa and her creative team on "Blade Runner 2099," Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049" is basically the poster child for legacy sequels done right. Rather than simply retread all the same ground as before (looking at you, "Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens"), "Blade Runner 2049" moved the story forward and took some seriously substantial risks along the way.

According to recent reports, according to Luisa, this gave her all the permission she needed to follow in its footsteps and take things in bold fresh directions with her show. "That freed us up in a lot of different ways, because it meant we weren't just beholden to repeating the same thing over and over again," she explains. One massive wrinkle in the Prime Video series is the fact "Blade Runner 2099" takes place after a Replicant uprising has shaken up the status quo, putting humans at the bottom of the food chain for once. It's a strange dynamic that our two main characters Olwen (the Replicant Blade Runner played by Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (the human posing as a Replicant played by Hunter Schafer) are forced to navigate throughout the season.

Industry observers note that as fans tune in, they can rest assured in the knowledge that the series is taking its cues from one of the most ambitious and boundary-pushing legacy sequels of them all. You could do a lot worse than that. All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are now on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways
