  • According to recent reports, to use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat.
  • Recent findings suggest that of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, google loves a rebrand. What started off as "Spark" is now "Task" in Gemini—not to be confused with Google Tasks, the to-do app. Google took its Spark AI agent, which used to live in a separate tab, and integrated it into the Gemini interface. Gemini Task is available globally, and it’s completely free to use for some. That stated, some features are limited to the U.S. and, of course, subject to some pretty strict usage limits. While not exactly a replacement for ChatGPT Dots or Meta Muse, you can think of Gemini Task as a controlled version of an AI agent that can do quite a lot in the background.

According to recent reports, to use Task, open Gemini and create a new chat. You’ll see a Task tab next to Chat. Switch to it, and start writing your prompt. (You’ll also see some suggested options here.) Type your task or action and press "Send." The feature works best if you’ve already enabled Personal Intelligence on your Google account, and have connected services like Gmail, Google Drive, and Photos as well. You can then tag “@Gmail” to use your Gmail account, or even a third-party connector. Task natively supports automation, so you can say something like, "run this task once every day," and the AI will add it to your Scheduled Tasks section.

Recent findings suggest that of course, I did the thing that every AI demo wants you to do: I asked Gemini to create a daily morning briefing for me, highlighting all important emails, calendar appointments, and tasks. And, in my experience, it works really well. It reminded me of this article's due date, that I have a couple of pitches in my inbox to review, that a credit card bill is due soon, and that there are some holidays around the corner.

Recent findings suggest that gemini is very good at retrieving information from emails and taking action. For example, I created an automation that collects all my coffee orders for the month and presents the data in Google Sheets. I then asked Task to create a subscription manager for me. Instead of paying for a third-party app, it took a few minutes to collate the services I pay for into one list. It even accounted for the currency differences (some subscriptions are in USD, some in INR) and gave me a tally in INR, along with things like average monthly cost, and more.

While Gemini can connect to the open web, it's quite a hostile place right now for an AI bot. Websites are blocking agents from accessing their pages, which hinders their effectiveness. I asked Gemini to create a task that monitors the price of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones daily. For this, it asked my permission to spin up a remote browser, and loaded up Amazon, only to be blocked instantly. It did succeed in opening Croma though (a national retailer in India), but it took almost a minute for it to figure out that the price had not dropped below what I asked for. Would it be quicker and less resource-intensive if I did this myself? Yes, but the fact that Gemini can do this every evening like clockwork is the real advantage—as long as the websites comply, that is.

According to recent reports, if you're going to try Task in Gemini for free, there are some limitations you should know about. The free plan only lets you run tasks once per day, and you can’t be granular about the exact timing. (Paid Gemini plans have no such restrictions.) You can only run 10 tasks at the same time, while the limit is 50 tasks for AI Pro customers. Compute-based usage limits will also apply, based on your plan. The free access is right now live in India, the U.S., Canada, Australia, Japan, and South Korea.

According to recent reports, some features, though, are only for U.S. people. Gemini’s feature that lets you call businesses on your behalf is restricted to the States, as is the ability to forward emails to [email protected] to automatically turn the contents of the email into a task (like adding a college schedule to your calendar). U.S. users can also connect their Google Wallet account to set up payments at supported stores.

Sources indicate that gemini Task is not a proactive agent, nor is it trying to be. You still have to check the work. You have to approve any vital steps, and if a website blocks AI models, there’s not a lot Gemini can do about it. For someone like me, who’s all-in on the Google ecosystem, I do see value in Gemini Task. The deep and robust Gmail integration is worth it alone. If you’re on the free blueprint, set up a couple of background tasks related to Gmail, Google Drive, or background research that run every morning, and call it a day. And if you’re paying for AI Pro, you can get a lot more done.

According to recent reports, indieWire, the definitive outlet for creative independence in film and TV, announced on Wednesday, November 25 the final additions to the lineup for the Winter 2026 edition of our IndieWire Honors event, featuring our largest lineup yet of film honorees. Curated and selected by IndieWire’s editorial team, IndieWire Honors is a celebration of the filmmakers, actors, and artisans key to crafting some of the most exciting cinematic works this year.

According to recent reports, the newly declared honorees include “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and costume designer Trish Summerville, who will be receiving the Spotlight Award. They join previously announced honorees John Turturro, Monica Barbaro, Andrew Garfield, Ike Barinholtz, Yura Borisov, James Gray, Adam Driver, Beth de Araújo, Mason Reeves, Gemma Chan, Ruth Madeley, David Greaves, Javier Ambrossi, Javier Calvo, Jeon Do-yeon, Anthony Ippolito, James Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, Mag Sarnowska, Paul Lambert, and Travis Knight. Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’.

Additionally, IndieWire has revealed that the incoming awards ceremony will be hosted by writer and comedian Demi Adejuyigbe, whose latest special “Demi Adejuyigbe Is Going to Do 1 (One) Backflip” is now available to stream on Dropout. Previous IndieWire Honors emcees include Emmy winner Alex Edelman, Emmy nominee Robby Hoffman, multi-hyphenate Dewayne Perkins, and lauded comedians Vinny Thomas and Atsuko Okatsuka.

In a recent development, indieWire Honors will take place on Thursday, December 3 in Los Angeles, starting with an intimate cocktail reception and awards ceremony. IndieWire will also begin rolling out exclusive editorial content, including honoree profiles, on Friday, November 27 through the lead-up to the awards night. Throughout the ceremony, into the next day, IndieWire will publish photos and exclusive social content from the event as well.

Industry observers note that “It’s thrilling to be able to recognize the artists behind so many of this year’s most exciting and compelling films,” noted Brent Lang, IndieWire’s editor-in-chief. “They dazzled us with their talent, inspired us with their willingness to take risks, and left an indelible mark on cinema. We are excited to celebrate their accomplishments.”.

“It’s exciting to celebrate such an eclectic group of film talent for this year’s IndieWire Honors,” noted James Israel, IndieWire’s SVP and Publisher. “We are also pleased to continue to celebrate top craft artisans in entertainment.”.

The Winter 2026 IndieWire Honors honorees are:.

Sources indicate that the fact that he is known for being a frequent collaborator of both Spike Lee and the Coen brothers conveys just how expansive an actor Turturro is. The Brooklyn native is quintessentially New York, as most recently proven in Sony Pictures Classics’ acclaimed Sundance premiere “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” written and directed by Noah Segan. Yet, a filmmaker can still drop the performer into the corporate dystopia of sci-fi series “Severance,” or have him go on a Southern odyssey in “O Brother, Where Art Thou?,” and he just as well hits it out of the park.

With nearly five decades of film work under his belt, starting with an uncredited role in “Raging Bull,” Turturro manages to be one of the few veteran actors who continues to best himself year after year.

The pair of Madrid-based directors colloquially known as Los Javis are not shy about cluing the audience in on the shoulders upon which they stand on. They cast Penélope Cruz and Lola Dueñas, two muses of auteur Pedro Almodóvar, as the most important women within their epic adaptation of an unfinished play by Federico García Lorca, another one of Spain’s queer artist forefathers. That reverence is balanced by the confidence in their own eye for newly introduced talent, weaving together three different timelines led by three relative unknowns, including most notably, indie musician Guitarricadelafuente, who also contributed the poignant original song “La Nieve” to the project.

Recent findings suggest that made outside the Hollywood system and chosen to represent Spain in the Best International Feature Oscar race, the Netflix release “La Bola Negra” is a film of immense scale. If viewers knew nothing of the director duo before seeing the film, they come away with a crash course in everything they are about. Considering how they won both the Best Director Award at Cannes, and the coveted People’s Choice Award at TIFF, it seems to be an experience most cinephiles enjoy.

“Tallgrass” is the code word that unlocks what makes the creative collaboration between “Paper Tiger” writer-director James Gray and star Adam Driver such a feat. Though the Neon release, which premiered at Cannes, is their first time ever working together, the filmmaker imbues the two-time Oscar nominee with such a specific vision of what it feels like to realize one’s time has gone by. Though the film is another deeply personal work in the oeuvre of the Queens-born auteur, Driver adds a more broad portrait of a figure wrapped up in crime, slowly feeling the overwhelming situation constrict and constrict.

“Josephine” was not made to be an easy watch, but boasts the rare feat of winning both the Grand Jury Prize and Audience Award at the Sundance Film Festival. Written and directed by Araújo, and starring Gemma Chan and Mason Reeves as mother and daughter, the drama is a bold exploration of how little control parents have over their children being confronted by certain horrors in life that there’s no guarantee of avoiding.

Sources indicate that an early release for fresh distributor Sumerian Pictures, “Josephine” has only felt more necessary as the year has gone on, and news stories like the Cornell rape case have come to the forefront. It is a conversation piece about a subject many wish to evade, that puts forth the effort to reach meaningful discourse.

In a recent development, the most bold artistic choice in “Artificial,” the latest film from prolific director Luca Guadagnino, is to not proffer any romance in becoming one of the Promethean figures. The repeated refrain of “Feel the AGI” rings as a benevolent threat by the time the two hours and 20 minutes of the Neon release are over. Garfield, Borisov, Barbaro, and Barinholtz, all four playing key figures in the genesis of OpenAI, play incredibly off of each other as tech titans forcing a smile as they convince their audience artificial technology is inevitable. Join or die. Their joint efforts to invoke a common sense of humanity would be funny if the reality of the situation weren’t so uncanny.

Recent findings suggest that re-teaming with her “Secret Sunshine” director Lee Chang-dong almost 20 years later, the “Possible Love” star is unmissable as a woman caught in a class divide between her blue collar, out-of-work husband, and the couple that hosts them as a means to interview them for a documentary. It is a role that she said uses “the whole entirety of her body” to push back against the weight of capitalism. The Netflix film chosen to represent South Korea in the Best International Feature category at the 2027 Oscars offers a feast of ideas, with Jeon’s layered turn as Mi-ok alone being enough fodder for many conversations to come.

According to recent reports, all sorts of biopics enter theaters each year, but few task their leads with the difficult job of playing someone still actively in the public eye. In Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky,” from Amazon MGM Studios, newcomer Ippolito deftly captures the distinctive look and sound of a young and hungry Sylvester Stallone. But what is more impressive than that form of transformation is how the 27-year-old actor captures the spirit of the unlikely star and scribe of the 1977 Best Picture winner. How some of his best moments come when he himself plays Rocky is a meta element we are still unpacking, but add it to the overwhelming evidence that Ippolito is one to watch.

It has been revealed that there is a standout moment in Oscar winner Siân Heder’s “Being Heumann” in which Madeley, as trailblazing disability rights activist Judy Heumann, asks a well-meaning congressman what he means by calling her “inspiring.” “Inspired to do what?,” she says. It is a moment that clarifies that the film about Heumann leading the successful protest to get the government to sign Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act is not standard fare about a woman in a wheelchair overcoming odds, but a film about her refusing to let those odds overcome her.

It has been revealed that madeley embodies a fight against circumstances that applies to more than just the disability community. May casting directors take notice of the limitless potential she offers as part of any type of ensemble.

As the President and CEO of Laika Studios, Knight has spent over 20 years educating audiences on the artform of stop-motion animation. And still, in his latest film “Wildwood,” a fantasy epic taking place in the forests outside Portland, Oregon, Knight directs scenes that seem inexplicable. It is hard enough to animate one bird flying, using that technique, yet the Fathom Entertainment release sees whole flocks fly off toward a war between species. The film’s commentary on parents and children is as heartrending as the craft behind how the film was made is genuinely inspiring to filmmakers of all types.

Industry observers note that talk about legacy. Decades after his father, noted documentarian William Greaves, hosted a party for the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” co-directed finished the film, one of the gems of Sundance 2026. To listen to Black luminaries from the ‘20s speak about how their work has endured into the ‘70s, with the dramatic irony of watching the film through a modern lens, is a singular cinematic experience. In a year where there is so much conversation around what pushes the documentary artform forward, the Neon release delivers both necessary context and innovation.

There is humor in having puppetry, one of the world’s oldest artforms, at the center of a conversation around innovation, but come on. Ortiz’s performance as Rocky in “Project Hail Mary,” supported by the work of visual effects team leaders Scanlan, Lambert, and Sarnowska, made us fall in love with a spidery alien rock that has no mouth or face. Puppetry’s forebearers would have still found that to be an insurmountable challenge. Hence, why the artist behind the fan favorite character opposite Ryan Gosling in the Amazon MGM Studios blockbuster deserves their flowers for helping viewers go beyond their earthly imaginations.

Though the latest film from director David Fincher and screenwriter Quentin Tarantino furthers the mis-adventures of Cliff Booth, the role that earned star Brad Pitt an Oscar, the Netflix film has an identity all its own. The work of costume designer Trish Summerville and actor Yahya Abdul-Mateen II are two elements that put that into focus, really easing the audience into the jump forward to 1977, where the silks flowed, and fur dripped off latest screen icons akin to the latter’s Rodrick “Hot Rod” Harrison. This go-round allows viewers to have an appreciation for more than just Hollywood, but the greater Los Angeles area, and all the distinct styles it brought in that pivotal ‘70s moment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that quentin Tarantino has returned to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" with "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" (why not read our review of the new movie here?). But this time, while Tarantino penned the script, he isn't in the director's chair. Instead, he's handed directing duties over to his pal David Fincher (who is ending his exclusive deal with Netflix with the film). Tarantino might not be behind the camera, but he still has a presence in the film, and it echoes something he did in "Hollywood" as well.

According to recent reports, early in "Cliff Booth," we're introduced to Charlie Peters, a hot-tempered TV star played by Scott Caan. To speed-run us through Charlie's successful career, we're given a little montage of his various roles, and that montage is narrated by none other than Tarantino, whose very recognizable voice provides some humorous details about Charlie's work.

Fans of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" will recall that Tarantino also provided narration in that movie, too. He actually wasn't the only narrator, either, because during one scene, Kurt Russell, who plays a stuntman named Randy in that film, also provides a little narration. As for Tarantino, he also voiced some crucial narration during a pivotal scene in "The Hateful Eight.".

It has been revealed that in fact, the filmmaker has a history of popping up in his movies, either via a voice cameo or a physical appearance. He has a pretty significant role in "Reservoir Dogs," makes a memorable cameo in "Pulp Fiction," gets to use an abysmal Australian accent in "Django Unchained," has his voice heard during a movie playing in "Inglourious Basterds" (and also plays a corpse in the film), plays a bartender in "Death Proof," portrays one of the members of the Crazy 88 gang in "Kill Bill," and lends his voice to an answering machine in "Jackie Brown.".

So while "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may not technically be a Quentin Tarantino movie, it still feels like one, right down to the obligatory cameo.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving has inspired some of the most beloved episodes in sitcom history. Between the pressure to prepare the perfect turkey, the complicated dynamics of extended families, and the inevitable dinner table disagreements, the holiday is a natural breeding ground for comedy.

Of course, the best Thanksgiving television episodes also capture the holiday's warmth and sentimentality. Some episodes have become iconic thanks to a particularly memorable visual gag or quotable line, while others are beloved for their emotional resonance. The episode's overall quality and the amount of Thanksgiving spirit packed in are equally notable.

According to recent reports, some sitcoms have practically claimed Thanksgiving as their own, making their annual holiday installments an event to remember. While shows like Friends and Bob’s Burgers could easily fill an entire list of the best Thanksgiving episodes on their own, this list includes just one holiday episode per sitcom.

From bona fide television classics to more modern instant hits, these episodes represent several decades of sitcom history. Whether they embrace the holiday's most vital theme, revel in the chaos, or explore the joy of new traditions with a chosen family, these universally loved Thanksgiving episodes are well worth watching each year.

It has been revealed that one of the underrated sitcoms of the 2010s, Fresh Off the Boat’s “Huangsgiving” is a charming addition that offers an immigrant family’s spin on a quintessentially American holiday. For the first time, Jessica and Louis host Jessica’s family for Thanksgiving at their Orlando home, with predictably chaotic results.

Recent findings suggest that jessica suspects her sister is manufacturing family drama to steal her thunder, while Louis overindulges with his brother-in-law instead of preparing dinner. Louis’ proposal to serve Cornish hens, which he considers the “personal pizza” of poultry, is a hilarious bit that snowballs into a scramble to procure a frozen turkey and an unfortunate mix-up involving the oven light.

Sources indicate that “Huangsgiving” is more of a screwball family comedy than an exploration of Thanksgiving traditions. However, the pressure to pull off the perfect holiday gathering is universally relatable, regardless of cultural background.

Seinfeld’s “The Mom & Pop Store” is a decidedly unconventional Thanksgiving episode, avoiding the traditional family dinner in favor of another American holiday institution: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Elaine helps her boss, Mr. Pitt, realize his lifelong dream of participating in the parade, while George becomes convinced he’s purchased a car previously owned by Jon Voight.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Kramer inadvertently puts a neighborhood shoe repair shop out of business, leaving Jerry without most of his shoes. The seemingly disparate storylines converge in spectacularly absurd fashion, demonstrating Seinfeld’s mastery of interconnected comedy.

While “The Mom & Pop Store” doesn’t embrace the sentimental trappings of Thanksgiving, that’s precisely what makes it such a classic Seinfeld holiday episode. From George’s celebrity obsession to Jerry’s accidental puncturing of the Woody Woodpecker balloon, the episode finds humor in the holiday's absurdities rather than its more wholesome traditions.

Full House’s “The Miracle of Thanksgiving” is one of the more sentimental sitcom Thanksgiving episodes, but its emotional sincerity is precisely what makes it so beloved. The Tanner family prepares to celebrate its first Thanksgiving since Pam’s death, with Danny, Jesse, and Joey attempting to recreate the holiday traditions she established.

When D.J. takes it upon herself to prepare the turkey, and Stephanie accidentally ruins the pumpkin pie, their efforts to replicate their mother’s Thanksgiving dinner prove disastrous. However, beneath the kitchen mishaps is a poignant story about a family navigating grief during a holiday that emphasizes togetherness.

Sources indicate that full House’s signature sentimentality is particularly effective for a holiday episode. “The Miracle of Thanksgiving” acknowledges how difficult the holidays can be after losing a loved one, showing that a meaningful family celebration doesn’t require a picture-perfect dinner.

Latest Girl established its tradition of chaotic Thanksgiving episodes early in its run. In the first season’s “Thanksgiving,” Jess decides to host a last-minute dinner at the loft as an excuse to invite a fellow teacher she has a crush on.

Much to her roommates’ chagrin, Jess’ enthusiasm for the gathering far exceeds her preparedness. From attempting to defrost a turkey in the dryer to discovering a dead body in a neighbor’s apartment, the disastrous dinner showcases the ensemble’s comedic chemistry.

It has been revealed that while New Girl doesn’t integrate the holiday into its narrative particularly elegantly, the episode’s conclusion, with the gang waiting in line for Black Friday (or, as Winston calls it, Friday), is a hilarious touch. The episode also captures the appeal of celebrating Thanksgiving with a dysfunctional found family.

It has been revealed that modern Family’s “Three Turkeys” is a masterclass in escalating holiday chaos. Phil takes charge of Thanksgiving dinner for the first time, but Claire, unconvinced of her husband’s culinary abilities, secretly prepares a backup turkey.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, Jay and Gloria pretend to be away for the holiday to enjoy some peace and quiet, while Mitchell insists that Cameron take a turn being the strict parent with Lily. There are, in fact, three turkeys and plenty of Three’s Firm-style hijinks afoot as the extended family’s little white lies snowball into an elaborate farce.

It has been revealed that thanksgiving led to some of the best Modern Family episodes because the holiday allowed characters’ individual neuroses to collide with hilarious consequences. While “Three Turkeys” uses Thanksgiving as a fairly generic holiday setting for its more emotional beats, the comedy surrounding the pressures of hosting and navigating competing family expectations makes it a particularly relatable holiday installment.

It may not be a traditional sitcom, but Master of None's season 2 Emmy-winning “Thanksgiving” is too exceptional to leave off this list. The gorgeous standalone episode chronicles Denise (Lena Waithe) and Dev’s (Aziz Ansari) friendship across decades of Thanksgiving celebrations, following Denise’s journey of coming to terms with her sexuality and coming out to her family.

According to recent reports, co-written by Waithe and Ansari and inspired by Waithe’s own experiences, “Thanksgiving” is an honest portrayal of why holidays can be so emotionally complicated. Revisiting the same family dinner table over the years is an inspired narrative device, illustrating how familial relationships evolve even when traditions remain the same.

It has been revealed that while other beloved Thanksgiving episodes mine family dysfunction for laughs, Master of None finds humor and humanity in the messiness of unconditional love. It’s an episode that will make viewers cry and want to call their moms.

Sources indicate that few sitcom characters take Thanksgiving as seriously as Bob Belcher, whose enthusiasm for the holiday has made Bob’s Burgers’ annual Thanksgiving episodes a beloved tradition in their own right. In “Turkey in a Can,” Bob’s meticulous preparations are repeatedly sabotaged when his carefully brined turkeys mysteriously wind up in the toilet.

It has been revealed that what begins as an absurd whodunit culminates in a surprisingly touching revelation about Bob’s anxiety over Tina growing up. Meanwhile, Bob’s increasingly awkward interactions with a grocery store butcher as he repeatedly purchases replacement turkeys provide some of the episode’s funniest moments.

Recent findings suggest that “Turkey in a Can” is the best episode of Bob's Burgers because it finds genuine emotional resonance in utterly ridiculous circumstances. Bob’s unwavering commitment to Thanksgiving dinner, despite his mounting frustrations, is a testament to how preparing food is his love language.

How I Met Your Mother’s “Slapsgiving” combines classic sitcom antics, HIMYM lore, and holiday sentimentality into 22 glorious minutes. As Marshall and Lily prepare to host their first Thanksgiving as a married couple, Marshall takes sadistic pleasure in psychologically tormenting Barney, counting down to the third slap of their infamous slap bet.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Ted and Robin struggle to navigate their friendship following their breakup, threatening to disrupt the gang’s holiday festivities. The episode strikes a delightful balance between the emotional growing pains of adulthood and the wonderfully juvenile antics that define the group’s dynamic.

Recent findings suggest that marshall’s musical performance of “You Just Got Slapped” is one of the most memorable payoffs to a running gag in How I Met Your Mother. By establishing Slapsgiving as one of How I Met Your Mother's unique holiday traditions, the episode also celebrates the joy of creating upcoming memories with a chosen family.

Cheers’ “Thanksgiving Orphans” is one of the most iconic Thanksgiving episodes in sitcom history, perfectly encapsulating the classic NBC comedy's enduring appeal. With the gang’s respective holiday intends falling through, Carla reluctantly hosts Thanksgiving dinner at her house.

However, mounting frustration over an interminably slow-cooking turkey culminates in a spectacular food fight, complete with a memorable glimpse of Norm’s notoriously unseen wife, Vera. The episode showcases the ensemble’s impeccable comedic timing, but its premise also captures the essence of Cheers.

If someone has nowhere else to go, they'll always have a place among the bar’s regulars. For all its slapstick comedy, “Thanksgiving Orphans” is a surprisingly poignant celebration of chosen family. The gang may drive one another crazy, but it's comforting knowing they’ll never have to spend the holidays alone.

Industry observers note that when it comes to sitcoms, Friends owns Thanksgiving. Several of the show's Thanksgiving installments could have comfortably topped this list, particularly “The One Where Ross Got High” and “The One With the Football.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, “The One With All the Thanksgivings” packs arguably the most Thanksgiving per minute of any sitcom episode. As the gang reminisces about their worst Thanksgivings, a series of hilarious flashbacks expands the characters’ shared history, from Chandler’s childhood holiday trauma to Monica and Chandler’s disastrous encounters in the '80s.

Recent findings suggest that the episode also delivers one of Friends’ most iconic romantic moments, with Chandler inadvertently professing his love for Monica while she dances with a turkey on her head. Between its ridiculous wigs, quotable dialogue, romantic developments, and genuine holiday sentimentality, “The One With All the Thanksgivings” is everything audiences could want from a sitcom Thanksgiving special.

Blade Runner 2099 Adds A Major Twist To The Classic Voight-Kampff Test

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I've seen spoilers you people wouldn't believe.
  • What's a worse fate in the world of "Blade Runner," to be human or to be a Replicant?
  • According to recent reports, leave it to "Blade Runner 2099" to flip yet another classic franchise staple on its head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I've seen spoilers you people wouldn't believe. This article discusses major plot details from all eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099.".

What's a worse fate in the world of "Blade Runner," to be human or to be a Replicant? Throughout both films, organics in this post-apocalyptic setting were able to "enjoy" their time at the top of the food chain. That all changes in Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099," the live-action story taking place after the world order has been upended and our supposed underlings have gained all the power for themselves. While Replicants were built to be "more human than human," the subtle differences between the two kinds are all but impossible to detect — on the surface, at least. But, as we know, looks can be deceiving; what's underneath is another matter entirely.

According to recent reports, leave it to "Blade Runner 2099" to flip yet another classic franchise staple on its head. Traditionally, the purposefully off-putting questionnaire known as the Voight-Kampff test was meant to detect whether an individual is a Replicant or not. In the sci-fi series, the rise of the Replicants and the 50 years that have passed since "Blade Runner 2049" have introduced even more changes. Enter the Index Test, an inverted form of the established quiz. But rather than differentiate between the two beings, this test is meant to detect whether the subject has developed feelings of empathy towards humans.

Recent findings suggest that in Episode 5, titled "My Lord," we learn far more about this strange new setup than the show had previously revealed. All we ever saw was the unusually young human girl administering the test, the odd non sequiturs she posed to (supposed) Replicants like Hunter Schafer's Cora, and the results of whether they passed the baseline or not. But that, too, was only scratching the surface.

Of all the differences between humans and Replicants, empathy is the biggest of them all. "Blade Runner 2099" draws fairly stark lines in the sand between the two, with flesh-and-blood people now completely helpless before their bioengineered creations. But despite their physical advantages and killer instincts, Replicants' lack of a childhood means they're deficit in that crucial, compassionate emotion separating humans from all other living things. As we soon learn, however, Replicants can feel these strong feelings ... and actually fear it, too.

This is all summed up in the storyline involving Greta (Katelyn Rose Downey), the young human girl we learn has been sold off into indentured servitude and indoctrinated along with many others into administering Index Tests. Episode 5 peels back all the horrifying layers, showing us Greta's training under awfully unsettling circumstances. First, she's taken through a museum exhibit explaining the purpose and history of the Voight-Kampff test, used by human Blade Runners to hunt Replicants. Now, the newly introduced status quo means Replicants use this new Index Test to police their own kind — and, as one instructor explains, prevent any "emotional contagion" crossing over from humans to their Replicant overlords.

In a recent development, it's a fascinating idea with some pretty serious implications for our two main characters. Michelle Yeoh's Olwen is at the moment undergoing some serious emotional turmoil herself, as her search for the missing Replicant and her secret lover Marek (Johnny Harris) ends in his tragic death. Meanwhile, Cora's own emotional attachments makes it only a matter of time before her human identity is made known. As a result, every time they sit down for the Index Test makes for must-watch TV.

All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are streaming on Prime Video.

The 10 Best Book Endings of All Time, Ranked

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when you read a book, you're probably going to have to dedicate a whole bunch of time to it, unless it’s a novella or unless you're just a supernaturally fast reader.
  • Recent findings suggest that books don’t have to end amazingly to be great, since Frank Herbert honestly wasn’t very good at final chapters, but most of his Dune books are worth reading (most of them just sort of end abruptly, though to be fair, you can say the same about Jaws, and that’s a flawless movie regardless).
  • In a recent development, novellas were mentioned before, and here’s one, technically: Animal Farm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when you read a book, you're probably going to have to dedicate a whole bunch of time to it, unless it’s a novella or unless you're just a supernaturally fast reader. If you're in the latter camp, good on you. Also, lucky you. But hey, even if you're a fast reader, you're still going to want the destination to make the journey worth it. And if you're not a fast reader, then you're probably going to be even keener for the book you’ve spent a whole bunch of time on to end on a high note.

Recent findings suggest that books don’t have to end amazingly to be great, since Frank Herbert honestly wasn’t very good at final chapters, but most of his Dune books are worth reading (most of them just sort of end abruptly, though to be fair, you can say the same about Jaws, and that’s a flawless movie regardless). If you are after books with amazing endings, though, then the ones below are definitely worth checking out. If a book below ends surprisingly, then the fact the ending is surprising will be noted, but the specifics of the surprise won’t be. So, consider that a warning that there might be some mild spoilers (but nothing too in-your-face) below.

In a recent development, novellas were mentioned before, and here’s one, technically: Animal Farm. Still, there’s a lot here packed into a relatively small number of pages, making Animal Farm more engaging and deep than a good many genuinely lengthy novels, because even if it’s technically about some animals on a farm (shock, horror) fighting for power, it’s actually about a whole lot more than that.

According to recent reports, or, more accurately, it’s about what you want it to be, depending on how you choose to break it down and all. In any event, the ending of Animal Farm packs a punch, even with it being the kind of thing that’s so iconic, it’s unlikely to count as a twist anymore. It happens, after so many years. It’s not quite the same as complaining about someone spoiling what happens by way of a massive natural disaster in the Book of Genesis (“Noah way,” people would say, if you could actually ruin it for them), but it’s also eventually not going to be too far off.

Sometimes known as The Golden Compass, Northern Lights is the first book in the His Dark Materials trilogy, and because that whole trilogy ends a bit unusually, it probably has the strongest ending out of any of the books. That feels a little odd to say, yet it is its own book, and without it ending the way it does, it might not be as likely that you'd feel so invested and ready to tackle the next two books right after this one’s done.

Basically, Northern Lights has a good number of shocking moments for a young adult (or even children’s, according to some sources) novel, and there are reveals here that are honestly surprisingly bleak. It feels conclusive for a part one, all the while leaving a lot open for the rest of the series to explore, but in a thankfully genuinely satisfying manner.

Recent findings suggest that before you get to the ending, 11.22.63 is about an English teacher who’s given the chance to go back in time, but specifically to 1958. He views this as an opportunity to stay in the past for a while, until the titular date, when John F. Kennedy was assassinated, and on that date, he intends to prevent the assassination from happening, which seems like it’ll change the future for the better... that’s the plan, at least.

And then the very end, without saying too much, does prove to be one of the most effortlessly emotional things Stephen King has ever written.

Much of 11.22.63 involves spending time to confirm who killed Kennedy while there, and then there are other forces that are harder to comprehend which seem to be working against him changing the past. When it gets to the end of things, though, it’s intense in a way that lives up to how suspenseful everything before the ending is, and then the very end, without saying too much, does prove to be one of the most effortlessly emotional things Stephen King has ever written in a very long (and mostly great) career.

Brandon Sanderson has such a knack for concluding his books on high notes that there’s a term for the climaxes he tends to write: a Sanderlance. Basically, you're hit with a whole lot of drama packed into the final stretch of almost any given novel of his, and since some of his books are quite long, you're sometimes looking at 100+ pages of grand-scale action and surprising reveals, all in rapid succession.

You can feel a Brandon Sanderson book is a little slow-going at times, but then feel at ease that you're going to feel a sense of surprise (and, perhaps paradoxically, some unease) by the time you reach the last few chapters. Mistborn: The Final Empire might well have the most powerful Sanderlanche to date, and like with Northern Lights and its place within His Dark Materials, the way The Final Empire concludes is almost guaranteed to make you intrigued about how the next two Mistborn books might play out.

If Blood Meridian ever got made into a movie, it would ultimately be one of the most grueling and bloody of all time, even if it was just a fraction as violent as its source material. Also, Judge Holden would probably enter the ranks of the best monsters in cinema history, but as it stands, he has to settle for being one of the most memorable monstrous characters in literary history, since he is far and away the worst of a bad bunch.

Since it’s Cormac McCarthy being talked about, the notion that the Judge is one of the only people to emerge from Blood Meridian unscathed shouldn’t be too surprising, and it’s also the kind of book where you know it’s all going to end miserably about 10 or so pages in (or perhaps even earlier). Everything you’ve heard about this book and the ways it’s controversial are true, and while it is worth reading if you’ve got a strong enough stomach, definitely don’t read it if you're uncomfortable with a book that ends without even a hint of hope or anything approaching redemption for any of its characters.

Unpredictability is at play throughout the entirety of House of Leaves, which has the distinction of being incredibly intense for much of its duration while being, at some other points, honestly a little slow. There are things here that deliberately draw the novel as a whole out, and House of Leaves isn't afraid to slow down its pacing, and if you want to really get lost in some of the text that isn't strictly about the main part of the story, you can get distracted for a while. Thankfully, though, it does end up rewarding your time.

The ending helps in that regard, even if there are still quite a few unanswered questions when all is said and done, to say the least. There are a whole bunch of different narratives within House of Leaves (before even getting to how oddly the whole novel’s presented), so it’s not the kind of thing that wraps up neatly… though it does wrap up powerfully and memorably, admirably delivering more than just horror at the story’s end (even if horror is the genre ultimately explored most effectively in the bulk of House of Leaves).

Sources indicate that stoner is a book about a man living a life and that’s about it, but also, that’s everything, because that’s life. That could make Stoner something of a hard sell, but then again, at the same time, it’s hard to imagine too many people reading it and not getting anything out of it. The titular character grapples with the highs and lows of life, with more of an emphasis on the lows, and he overcomes a little but mostly just endures a whole lot.

As a result, Stoner ends the way it always had to, because it’s a life story, beginning with the main character’s early stages of life and then ending when that life is no more. To say Stoner is ruinable would be like someone saying that learning they're going to die is a life spoiler. Finding meaning before that inevitable end is what's vital, and that is what you get here (and it’s also what William Stoner thankfully finds, at least to some extent).

Before addressing or alluding to the ending, it has to be stressed that And Then There Were None has one of the best premises of all time, and then part of the reason it’s here is that the quality of the ending matches the quality of the premise. It’s immense all the way through, in other words, being perhaps the ultimate Agatha Christie novel, and one about ten people being told to go to an island and dying one by one.

Industry observers note that because they're all isolated, those who don’t die initially have to try to figure out who’s doing the murdering, and then, unsurprisingly, you, as a reader, are likely hooked. Of all the books here, it would feel like the biggest crime to ruin And Then There Were None, even with it being close to 90 years old, at the time of writing. It’s a fast-paced and relatively short book, too, so there’s little excuse not to read it, even if you're not exactly the biggest fan of reading in the world.

Like with The Stand and IT, which are some other classic (and lengthy) books by Stephen King, some people really don’t seem to like how The Dark Tower, as a series, concluded with the seventh main book, which was fittingly called The Dark Tower VII: The Dark Tower. It’s bold for sure, perhaps to a greater extent than even the ending found in IT, which might well be the only “more” controversial Stephen King ending in a career filled with somewhat divisive finales, but let it be known: these books have genuinely great endings.

There was a need to wrap up a lot here, and with The Dark Tower VII, Stephen King didn’t pull any punches, and then he also didn’t limit himself in terms of strange and offbeat ideas. There’s a sense of overwhelming finality here, alongside some admittedly anticlimactic (but in a purposeful way) elements, and then also a lot that’s surprisingly meta and introspective. It gives you a ton to think about and feel all at once, and it’s undoubtedly striking as a grand finale, proving difficult to forget and/or shake, for better or worse.

Whatever decade it had been published in, it’s inevitable that The Lord of the Rings would have been the top of that decade. It is just something special, so even if that’s a bit expected, and also maybe a bit boring to put it in the number one spot here, sorry, but it’s The Lord of the Rings. It has a bit of everything, including great characters, an immense world, a well-paced epic narrative, and a surprising amount of emotional weight.

Sources indicate that lots of the emotion comes at the end, expectedly, though by no means should The Lord of the Rings only be read for its ending (you'll realize sooner rather than later how good the journey is, almost regardless of the destination). There’s a whole lot of drama here, and a good many characters, but all the events and all those character arcs come to beyond-fitting conclusions by the time the whole epic novel wraps up (it’s a lengthy ending, especially if you read all those appendices, but undeniably worth it).

Sources indicate that one of Apple’s most beloved products this year was undoubtedly the MacBook Neo. Unlike some of its other budget products, Apple seems interested in updating the MacBook Neo on an annual cycle, and we may get the next MacBook Neo around March.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is targeting the iOS/macOS 27.4 release cycle for the release of the new MacBook Neo, as well as the A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and OLED iPad Air.

While he notes that this cycle runs between February and March, it doesn’t necessarily mean the products will launch on the earlier end of that spectrum. Apple is also expected to release the iPhone Air 2, OLED iPad Air, and a newly introduced iPad Pro within the first half of the year, but they’ll likely come a bit later than the aforementioned products.

As expected, the next MacBook Neo will bump up from the A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM to the A19 Pro chip with 12GB of RAM.

According to recent reports, apple will also introduce new colors on the MacBook Neo “frequently,” though it’s unclear if we’ll see that with the next iteration. From the Power On newsletter:.

According to recent reports, the other thing I’ve heard is that Apple plans to refresh the MacBook Neo’s colors frequently. We’ll see if that trend starts with the first follow-up.

I’m certainly excited to see the next generation MacBook Neo, especially with 12GB of unified memory. While 8GB is certainly fine, heavy multitaskers will notice it, especially with unoptimized software.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger question is: will the next MacBook Neo have a price increase? With additional RAM included, it feels inevitable.

Hopefully backlit keyboard if they increase price.

Apple increased the price of MacBook Neo from $599 to $699 back in June, and in October the company also silently decreased the education discount by $50, meaning the education price has increased from $499 to $649 since launch.

In a recent development, if there is a price increase, it likely won’t be too major, maybe $50 – leaving the computer at $749. Compared to the rest of the laptop landscape, MacBook Neo would still be a good value. We’ll see what happens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A posh, Philippine country club’s colonial secrets are exposed in Rafael Manuel’s evocatively creepy, grimly funny, and austerely constructed social satire, “Filipiñana,” set outside Manila.

Sources indicate that writer/director Rafael Manuel’s film, which won a World Cinema special jury award at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival, also stands a chance at being his country’s first representative on a Best International Feature Film Oscar shortlist. While the Philippines was among the eight countries that submitted during the category’s inaugural year in 1956 (with Lamberto V. Avellana’s “Child of Sorrow”) along with France, Italy, and others, it’s never been nominated or shortlisted. Related Stories IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Massive Christmas Expansion.

Industry observers note that executive-produced by Manuel’s former mentor Jia Zhangke, “Filipiñana” follows a tee girl who discovers something is off (and downright sinister) about the club’s administration, specifically president Dr. Palanca (Teroy Guzman). She’s played by Jorrybell Agoto, who, at just 32 years old, died earlier in November after a short battle with lymphoma.

In a recent development, indieWire’s interview with filmmaker Rafael Manuel took place a week before the news, though he shared in a later statement, “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorybell’s family, who have just lost a loving ate [the Filipino word for older sister] and a devoted daughter.”.

An elegaic air, too, hangs over the film in retrospect and even before Agoto’s passing, as “Filipiñana” dwells in ghosts of the Philippines’ imperial past and Spanish occupation.

“No one explains it to you beforehand,” director Manuel told IndieWire of touring with his first feature for nearly a year. (We spoke over Zoom while he smoked a cigarette in his Amsterdam apartment.) “What I’m starting to realize is the biggest difference between short and feature is that with short festival, it’s kind of the end goal. When you premiere at your festival, you’re so happy, and it’s done; it’s like people get to see it finally. But with a feature film, it’s just the beginning, and no one explained this to me.”.

Manuel joins the ranks of Lav Diaz, Brillante Mendoza, the late Lino Brocka, and many others to represent the Philippines at the Academy Awards — a concept, he mentioned, that was never really on his radar.

Recent findings suggest that “When we were coming up with this film and the genesis of the film, you don’t really think about an Oscars race,” stated Manuel. “You just think about making the best film you can. And especially coming from Southeast Asia, access to the American market, even getting a U.S. theatrical release, it’s not something that’s very common. Usually, your usual route is via the European arthouse market. So it’s been really surprising and in the best way possible, seeing how well received the film is in the States, in North America, and in the Anglo world in general.”.

Sources indicate that the process was a “very challenging one,” he remarked, as the Philippines is taking the Oscar push very seriously from a governmental perspective. “And to be the first film that’s seriously backed by the government means a lot to us,” he said, especially for a film that’s critical of government and social hierarchy.

And there are hat tips not only to Jacques Tati, but also to Wes Anderson and Michael Haneke, at least in reviews, in terms of the movie’s flattened remove from violence and its dryly observational approach where everything in the frame is meticulously arranged.

“I get why people are saying Michael Haneke and Wes Anderson,” he mentioned. “I mean, Jacques Tati, obviously, he’s a really significant influence for me, but for example, with Haneke, I feel like we tackle violence very differently from how Haneke tackles violence. And I think with Wes Anderson, I see it because of the colors, because of the symmetrical framing and all of that, but I think this is very much a satire of that. And so, yes, we use a lot of Western codes and Western aesthetics in the film, but because it’s a film that deals with Western influence in the Orient, it was a film that deals with colonization. So the form and the aesthetic of the film is very much part of the satire. It’s the form.”.

He added, “It’s a polarizing film. I think it’s either you love it or you hate it, and I think that’s the same whether you’re in the West or in the Philippines.”.

The distribution of world cinema in the Philippines also helps to explain the divided palate for “Filipiñana,” as audiences have very little exposure to arthouse cinema from the outside world.

According to recent reports, “In the Philippines, distribution of world cinema, it’s almost nonexistent. In Metro Manila, we have basically one or two arthouse cinemas, independent cinemas. The rest of the cinemas are all in shopping malls, and all they play are local rom-coms or Marvel movies,” he stated. But problems in the West of audience fatigue over shopworn, recycled I.P. and familiar material also apply in the Philippines.

In a recent development, “It’s been a hot topic lately in the Philippines and consumers and audiences complaining about formulaic Filipino filmmaking. They’re tired of the formulaic rom-coms. But then the thing is that in the Philippines, I would say 90 percent of people have never seen a Lav Diaz film, even maybe 99 percent of people haven’t seen a Lav Diaz film,” Manuel stated of the slow cinema master behind last year’s submission, the Gael García Bernal-starring “Magellan,” which also dealt in the Philippines’ colonized history. (Diaz and Manuel share producers, including Bianca Balbuena and Bradley Liew, though they’ve never actually met.).

It has been revealed that “Filipiñana” marks a break from tradition in terms of its Westernized style — and chatter has been flying on Letterboxd over the film since the Sundance premiere. (“I look through Letterboxd sometimes. Well, I used to, I stopped. And then the unhealthy thing with Letterboxd, for me especially, is that I’ll skip all the good comments and I’ll just read all the bad comments,” he stated.).

“When you’re faced with something different with arthouse cinema, like Filipino arthouse cinema, when Filipino audiences are faced with Filipino arthouse cinema, and you get some violent reactions, then it begs the question, ‘When you’re complaining about being tired of formulaic Filipino filmmaking, what exactly do you mean, and what exactly is it that you want?’ Do you just want Hollywood films but with brown faces in them? Because I don’t think that’s the answer either.”.

“Filipiñana” is now streaming on Kino Film Collection.

#132518. Blade Runner 2099 Proves The Saga Does One Thing Better Than Any Other Sci-Fi Franchise

Blade Runner 2099 Proves The Saga Does One Thing Better Than Any Other Sci-Fi Franchise

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that continuing the legacy of two of the greatest sci-fi movies ever made is a massive enough challenge.
  • It has been revealed that it's hard to imagine, but "Blade Runner" had a tiny VFX budget.
  • As such, when Denis Villeneuve managed to both emulate the feel of Scott's classic and push the production design in newly introduced directions with "Blade Runner 2049," it was nothing short of a miracle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that continuing the legacy of two of the greatest sci-fi movies ever made is a massive enough challenge. Doing so on the small screen adds an extra element of difficulty. Incredibly, "Blade Runner 2099" has overcome the odds to deliver yet another intoxicating excursion into the techno-industrial urban decay-scape so magically realized back in 1982's "Blade Runner" and so faithfully recreated in 2017's "Blade Runner 2049." As such, the Blade Runner franchise is now surely the most consistent on-screen sci-fi saga ever made. (Setting aside sci-fi sagas that are directed by the same person the whole time, like James Cameron's "Avatar.").

It has been revealed that it's hard to imagine, but "Blade Runner" had a tiny VFX budget. Yet director Ridley Scott and his production team managed to create one of the most believable and immersive worlds in cinema history. The famous "Hades" opening shot immediately plunges you into a future post-ecological collapse, in which technology seems to have almost grown on the wreckage of a fallen world like moss on fallen trees. The debris of society is adorned with neon and machinery, creating an environment in which past and future collide. "Blade Runner" might have been buried at the box office by "E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial," but it was an absolutely enthralling sci-fi adventure that came to define the genre.

As such, when Denis Villeneuve managed to both emulate the feel of Scott's classic and push the production design in newly introduced directions with "Blade Runner 2049," it was nothing short of a miracle. The "Dune" director's take on the world first introduced to audiences in 1982 was immediately familiar as the same one in which Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard did battle with Rutger Hauer's Roy Batty and his band of rogue Replicants. Yet it also felt appropriately evolved for the three-decade time jump. Surely "Blade Runner 2099" couldn't pull off the same trick — especially across eight episodes? Well, it has.

It has been revealed that /Film's Bill Bria has hailed "Blade Runner 2099" as the best sci-fi show in years, and it's hard to disagree based solely on the production design. From the moment the show begins, we're immersed in the same world to which Ridley Scott introduced us back in 1982. In fact, "2099" recreates the "Hades" sequence so faithfully you'd think you were watching the original. It's a clever move, too. As the camera slow-zooms on the Tyrell Corporation building and evokes the tone and feel of Scott's film, it establishes "2099" as very much belonging to the "Blade Runner" legacy. But we soon discover that this is not Rick Deckard's future.

80 years after Harrison Ford's Blade Runner absconded with Rachael (Sean Young), Replicants have now overthrown their human masters to become the dominant race. It's a major change that refreshes the franchise and helps make it more relevant than it's ever been at a time when the looming AI garbage future has prompted widespread talk of machines taking our jobs.

It has been revealed that as such, it's more notable than ever to maintain a tone and design language that's consistent with what came before, so as to reassure fans of the saga that this isn't some sort of wholesale reinvention of the franchise they love, but an evolution that plays out in the same world. "Blade Runner 2099" impressively pulls that off with its opening scene, and it only gets better from there.

Industry observers note that when it comes to the world of "Blade Runner," fans know the deal: Retro futurism and cyberpunk aesthetics meet noirish expressionism in a technological nightmare future. Many franchises have tried to emulate the aesthetic to varying degrees of success, but there is only one "Blade Runner." As Christopher Nolan once told the Directors Guild of America while discussing Ridley Scott's film, it conjures "that feeling that there was this whole world outside the frame of the scene. You really felt there were things going on outside of those rooms where you've seen the film take place.".

"Blade Runner 2099" has somehow managed to make every one of its scenes feel like they belong in that same world. With that in mind, it's truly remarkable how consistent the Blade Runner universe has remained across almost a half-century's worth of projects, each of which has been separated by many years. Even the best sci-fi franchises struggle to pull off what is, admittedly, an almost impossible trick.

The "Terminator" movies have never been able to recapture the intoxicating, doom-laden sci-fi slasher tone that made the first two films so memorable. The "Alien" franchise, meanwhile, has made a point of switching up its style and tone with each successive film — though more recent projects have tried to evoke the feeling of the 1979 original. "Blade Runner" films, however, all feel part of a cohesive whole that gives the entire saga this uncanny sense of existing in a real alternate timeline somewhere — as if we're witnessing an epic, decades-spanning dream play out in the mind of a dying Replicant. Regardless of how you feel about "2099" as a whole, its visual and tonal achievements simply can't be denied.

"Blade Runner 2099" Season 1 is now streaming on Prime Video.

Industry News: The One Reason Nintendo and Rockstar Can Make Games Like Ocarina of Time and GTA 6

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though wildly different in tone and scope, both Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto 6 and Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time exemplify the craft of making video games at its finest.
  • It has been revealed that nintendo has long been held up as an example of a organization that retains and cultivates talent.
  • Senior executives at Nintendo, including Iwata and Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto, have also famously taken pay cuts of up to 50% to prevent layoffs and preserve morale amid slow sales of the 3DS and Wii U consoles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though wildly different in tone and scope, both Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto 6 and Nintendo’s remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time exemplify the craft of making video games at its finest. Each one is redolent with attention to detail. Whether it’s the achingly nostalgic aesthetic of Ocarina or Rockstar’s Borg-like hive-mind of interconnected gameplay systems, there is a staggering amount of talent and dedication on display in these games. There are the kinds of endeavors that take years to pull off — and a tech giant dedicated to helping its employees learn and grow over time. These are not the sort of games that can be produced by a company that lays people off every six months.

It has been revealed that nintendo has long been held up as an example of a organization that retains and cultivates talent. Throughout the unrelenting flood of layoffs across the games industry over the last several years, a quote from former president Satoru Iwata has consistently made the rounds on social media. “If we reduce the number of employees for better short-term financial results, employee morale will decrease, and I sincerely doubt employees who fear that they may be laid off will be able to develop software titles that could impress people around the world,” Iwata mentioned back in 2013.

Senior executives at Nintendo, including Iwata and Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto, have also famously taken pay cuts of up to 50% to prevent layoffs and preserve morale amid slow sales of the 3DS and Wii U consoles. And it seems to have worked. According to a Fortune report from December 2025, Nintendo of Japan has a staggering 98% employee retention rate, meaning that an employee stays at least three years. The average employee stays at the company for 15 years. That figure is only slightly less impressive at Nintendo of America, which boasts a 95% employee retention rate.

When people stay at a company for a decade or longer, upcoming employees are able to learn from seasoned masters. In Nintendo’s case, that means the Ocarina remake was developed by more junior staff, with guidance from veterans like Eiji Aonuma (who directed the original game and three other installments of the Zelda series) and Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom director Hidemaro Fujibayashi. Capcom’s delightful Pragmata is another 2026 example of senior talent training up a new generation of developers to create something fresh in the increasingly stagnant AAA space. Meanwhile, it seems that most American companies would rather cut an eight- or nine-figure bonus check to a CEO for forward-thinking strategies like culling 5% of employees every quarter, refusing to give up on trends that died years ago, or ravenously gobbling up smaller studios only to shutter them a couple years later. (Yes, EA, Sony, Xbox, and Epic Games. I’m talking about you.).

It has been revealed that perhaps not all American studios are quite so mercenary. Rockstar is headquartered in Scotland, but its parent tech giant, Take-Two Interactive, is based in the US. And it seems that a major reason GTA 6 has managed to live up to more than a decade’s worth of hype and stratospheric expectations is that the company has been willing to invest in staff for the long term. In an interview published on the heels of GTA 6’s Nov. 19 release, Bloomberg reported that about 21% of employees at Rockstar Games (around 1,000 people from a staff of roughly 4,700) had been with the company for more than 10 years.

Recent findings suggest that in an Oct. 14 feature, Rockstar North co-head Aaron Garbut told Bloomberg, “the last 30 years have been practice for where we got to here. The team and us as individuals have been doing it for so long that there’s a sort of shared understanding, shared knowledge and a sort of shortcut to questions.” That shared knowledge is a major reason core gameplay elements like the heat and honor systems in GTA 6 feel like significant evolutions over GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2. Rockstar wasn’t starting from scratch, because many of the people who created those earlier systems were still with the tech giant.

There are plenty of caveats to consider with all of this. Japan has far stricter labor laws that are designed to protect employees. People there also have access to universal healthcare. Game dev salaries are generally lower in Japan than in the US and Europe. All of those things make longer tenures at Japanese companies more likely. And Rockstar doesn’t have an unblemished record when it comes to labor issues. Ahead of the launch of Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018, the tech giant was widely criticized after a Kotaku exposé called out its corporate “culture of crunch” that saw staffers working excessive overtime on nights and weekends for months on end. In the years since, the company has made significant strides toward preventing crunch and has nearly doubled its staff. However, in October 2025, Rockstar laid off 34 staffers, alleging they had shared company secrets. Those former workers later accused Rockstar of union busting.

Yet even after GTA 6 officially became the biggest entertainment debut of all time, selling an estimated 44.9 million copies and earning more than $4 billion in just four days, Rockstar employees are still concerned about their job security and working to unionize. In a Nov. 18 opinion piece for The Guardian, animation programmer Nestor Uriarte wrote, “It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organized.”.

Let’s all hope that Rockstar doesn’t take a page from some of the industry’s worst actors and lay off the very people responsible for making the company a staggering amount of money over the last several days. But in the meantime, let’s also acknowledge that 2026 has given us two of the best video games of all time in GTA 6 and the Ocarina of Time remake. That level of excellence simply cannot come from treating developers, writers, and artists like they’re expendable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that barbara Gordon, the classic Batgirl, gets her coolest art ever, and her iconic costume is nowhere in sight. For close to 60 years, Barbara Gordon has been an integral member of the Bat Family, be it as Batgirl or Oracle. At the moment, Barbara is in the fight of her life in the fresh Breakout maxiseries, but it also gives her some truly awesome art.

Initially created to tie in with the then in-production Batman television series, Batgirl first appeared in 1967’s Detective Comics #359, debuting in the program around that time as well. The daughter of Commissioner Gordon, Barbara became Batgirl and fought crime alongside Batman and Robin. Then, in 1988’s The Killing Joke, the Joker shot Barbara, paralyzing her from the waist down. Undaunted, Barbara became Oracle, which allowed her to utilize her background in information science, serving as an information broker for the heroes of the DC Universe.

Batgirl was created by television producer William Dozier, writer Gardner Fox, artist Carmine Infantino and editor Julius Schwartz.

Recent findings suggest that barbara resumed her career as Batgirl at the beginning of the Fresh 52 era, but has since stepped back from the spotlight. Earlier this year, as part of its Next Level initiative, DC released Barbara Gordon: Breakout. Written by Mariko Tamaki and drawn by Amancay Nahuelpan, Breakout sees Gordon sent to prison. Yet there is far more going on just below the surface, and she is getting to the bottom of it all. It will be a struggle for Barbara, but it is also providing some awesome art in the process.

In a recent development, DC Comics has released its solicitations for books shipping in February, including Barabra Gordon: Breakout #10, by the book’s regular creative team of Tamaki and Nahuelpan. DC released a plot synopsis for Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10, which reads as follows:.

Barbara Gordon entered Supermax to save inmates from an unknown killer. But after last issue’s shocking revelations, she may have doomed everyone within the prison’s walls. With the clock counting down, can she stop the bloodbath before it begins? Or has her quest to rescue some of the prisoners doomed them all?

The book will ship with variant covers by Taurin Clarke and Francesco Tomaselli.

Of particular interest is the main cover for Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10. Drawn by Jorge Fornes, the cover depicts Gordon, battered and bandaged up, diving from the top of the prison she is being held in, all while a massive explosion happens above her. The implication is Barbara has escaped from prison, and the bad guys have been punished.

Yet perhaps the most noteworthy aspect of the cover for Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10 is what the titular heroine is wearing. Her traditional Batgirl costume is nowhere to be seen. Instead, she wears the standard jumpsuit of an inmate. The sight of the law-abiding Barbara Gordon dressed as a convict might scramble the brains of some, but it actually makes perfect sense.

Industry observers note that the cover to Barbara Gordon: Breakout #10 makes an vital point about the character: that her heroism transcends whatever codename or handle she is using at the time. As a child, she watched her parents drift apart and her brother descend into madness. Witnessing such sights young could have caused Barbara to become a hateful recluse. However, she channeled this anger and outrage in a positive way, becoming Batgirl and one of Bruce’s most trusted allies.

Some fans argue that Barbara did not come into her own until she became Oracle, as it helped her truly escape Batman’s shadow.

Sources indicate that then, when life dealt her a bad hand, she made the best of it by becoming Oracle in 1989’s Suicide Squad #23. Some fans argue that Barbara did not come into her own until she became Oracle, as it helped her truly escape Batman’s shadow. At the time, there was no other character quite like Oracle in comics. Barbara has extensive training in library sciences. This, when coupled with her world-class hacking skills, made her a true asset for the Bat Family and DC’s heroic community as a whole.

Sources indicate that and Barbara's actions in Breakout have driven home the notion that she does not need a heroic codename or a Batgirl outfit to be awesome. Barbara entered prison intending to help people, and while the cover to Breakout #10 casts doubt on whether she is successful, it is still a spectacular image, capturing everything great about the character. Even though the Batgirl suit is nowhere in sight, Gordon is still bringing the intensity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".
  • In a recent development, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is not a direct sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," as we knew from Quentin Tarantino handing over the director's chair to David Fincher.
  • Part of the appeal of returning to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is that the movie ended by changing history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

In a recent development, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is not a direct sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," as we knew from Quentin Tarantino handing over the director's chair to David Fincher. But still, you had to wonder if any other familiar faces would pop up in this latest mis-adventure.

Part of the appeal of returning to the world of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is that the movie ended by changing history. Thanks to the actions of Cliff, actress Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie) is not murdered by the Manson family. How does the entertainment world and Los Angeles change by 1977, when "Cliff Booth" takes place, because of that ripple effect? Tarantino wrote the script for "Cliff Booth," and if any filmmaker is equipped to dig into the nitty-gritty of such a change in Hollywood history, down to the most obscure B-pictures and forgotten TV, it's him.

Now, the major supporting cast of "Cliff Booth" is totally different. Cliff's best friend, actor Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) — for whom Cliff worked as a stunt double and driver back in 1969 — does not appear due to DiCaprio declining a cameo appearance. The movie mentions a few times that Rick moved to Australia and is presently starring in a popular TV show there, "Dingo Dan." Tarantino has also devised some stories about what happened to Rick after that fateful August 9, 1969 night.

But a few of the fictionalized Hollywood characters return for brief cameos: Margot Robbie as Sharon Tate, Timothy Olyphant as actor James Stacy, and even Nicholas Hammond as TV director Sam Wanamaker (in a smaller role).

It has been revealed that one of the Quentin Tarantino Easter eggs in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes, a fictional brand that appears in other Tarantino movies. The actress in the commercial is Sharon Tate, with Cliff smiling at her and likely recalling how he saved her life. "Once Upon A Time In Hollywood" cast Sharon Tate in an angelic light, down to giving her the happy ending that reality didn't. But revisiting her in greater depth, like what became of her marriage to Roman Polanski or how her acting career played out, would risk adding a dash of salt to that sweet ending.

Sources indicate that the alternate history of Sharon Tate in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" earned obvious comparisons to Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," which also starred Brad Pitt (as Lieutenant Aldo Raine, leader of the Nazi-killing Basterds). In that movie, Adolf Hitler (Martin Wutke) dies at the hands of Jewish soldiers instead of by suicide. That leads into Timothy Olyphant's "Cliff Booth" cameo, which feels self-recursively inspired by "Basterds.".

In a recent development, "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" mixes real Hollywood history with pastiche. Much of the first half sees Dalton filming a guest spot on a TV Western, "Lancer," which was a real show back in the late '60s. Olyphant appears as the real-life star of "Lancer," James Stacy, and the episode is directed by Nicholas Hammond's Sam Wanamaker, the real director of the "Lancer" pilot episode. "Cliff Booth" gives us another glimpse of Stacy and Wanamaker working in this alternate timeline's television industry.

It has been revealed that since 1969, Cliff Booth has become a fixer: someone who (violently) solves problems for Hollywood fixtures wrapped up with criminals. Fictional TV star Charlie Winters (Scott Caan) becomes one of his clients. The movie includes a newsreel style montage, narrated by Quentin Tarantino himself, recounting Winters' rise to TV stardom.

Sources indicate that one of Winters' indicates is "Enemy Territory," about a U.S. pilot trapped behind enemy lines in Europe during World War 2. The narrator describes the show as "'The Fugitive' with Nazis, but 'The Fugitive' with Nazis is a fun idea." (I'd watch it!) We see Winters shooting a scene where his character threatens a Gestapo officer into helping him rescue a captured American general. The officer is played by none other than Timothy-Olyphant-as-James-Stacy, doing a broad German accent with a high pitch reminiscent of Christoph Waltz's Colonel Hans Landa from "Inglourious Basterds.".

Sources indicate that sam Wanamaker is directing the scene. Stacy's performance is being criticized as "a smidge cavalier" — so Winters puts a live round in the prop gun with which his character is threatening the Gestapo officer. Stacy, sure enough, begins acting like a man whose life is being balanced on the edge of a trigger.

Casting Olyphant as James Stacy was a nod to how his real most famous roles are on Western TV shows — namely, Sheriff Seth Bullock in HBO's "Deadwood" and Deputy U.S. Marshal Raylan Givens in the Kentucky-set neo-Western "Justified." But Olyphant has got range beyond playing cowboys, and his comic energy in his "Cliff Booth" cameo is just more evidence of that.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is playing in theaters, with a Netflix release date of December 23, 2026.
