This 1996 classic comedy is the best movie to watch on Thanksgiving – and it's not even a Thanksgiving movie

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deck the halls with family drama … fa-la-la-la-awkward.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The Birdcage” came out in 1996, yet 30 years later, it couldn’t be more relatable.
  • The Mike Nichols-directed film is certainly a product of its time, yet nearly a decade before “Brokeback Mountain,” it did far more for LGBTQ+ inclusivity than the infamous cowboy flick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deck the halls with family drama … fa-la-la-la-awkward. You don’t need Thanksgiving to start an argument at the dinner table, though it is the ultimate excuse to air every grievance you’ve suppressed since that doomed Fresh Year’s resolution to "be more zen." (Spoiler alert: It didn’t stick.).

Recent findings suggest that “The Birdcage” came out in 1996, yet 30 years later, it couldn’t be more relatable. Sure, it isn't marketed as a Thanksgiving movie, nor does it take place during the holiday. Still, the Robin Williams classic centers on a high-stakes family dinner showdown, serving sus soup — and plenty of political in-law drama — in bowls decked out with naked men. That kind of spice puts memaw’s pumpkin pie to shame.

The Mike Nichols-directed film is certainly a product of its time, yet nearly a decade before “Brokeback Mountain,” it did far more for LGBTQ+ inclusivity than the infamous cowboy flick.

The premise of “The Birdcage” sounds like an alpha-male podcaster’s worst nightmare: What happens when the not-so-demure daughter of a right-wing politician marries the son of a gay cabaret owner and his drag queen partner?

Recent findings suggest that there’s meeting the parents, and then there’s meeting your future son-in-law’s dad and his "wife" — who happens to be Albert in drag. Robin Williams anchors the film as doting dad Armand, while Nathan Lane plays Albert, his longtime partner. Their on-screen dynamic swings from heartfelt and wholesome to wildly theatrical without ever tipping into pure parody. Dan Futterman also brings an exasperated charm to Armand’s son, groom-to-be Val — no small feat for a guy asking his dad to step back into the closet to appease his future in-laws. Not cool, Val.

The "meet the parents" trope wasn't exactly fresh in ’96; the movie was adapted from Jean Poiret’s 1973 play, “La Cage aux Folles.” Yet Gene Hackman as ultra-conservative Senator Keeley, Dianne Wiest as his wife Louise, and Calista Flockhart as bride-to-be Barbara bring an unexpected edge to a rocky family dynamic (featuring some mild repression). Even Hank Azaria (Agador) and Christine Baranski (Katharine) steal every scene they’re in. The best part? Vocally homophobic Senator Keeley seems to have a bit of a thing for Albert in a wig. Who’s going to tell him?

It has been revealed that beneath the farce and political clash sits a relatable story about identity, loyalty and fighting for love that hits hard during Thanksgiving and the endless gauntlet of holiday obligations that follow. Even if you think the Goldmans are way too lenient on the Keeleys (yeah, hi), it’s always easier to watch someone else’s family meltdown than to survive your own.

Industry observers note that you can certainly argue that “The Birdcage” isn’t perfect. It leans a little too heavily into femme stereotypes, traditional gender roles and "let's just agree to disagree" diplomacy at the queer characters' expense. Three decades on, though, it still feels like a movie that celebrates the queer community rather than treating us as the punchline, which is more than I can say for prestige dramas like “Brokeback Mountain” that double down on queer tragedy and shame. I usually champion queer stories led by creatives from the community, yet “The Birdcage” used its star-studded cast to pull mainstream audiences into an early, unapologetic celebration of queer joy.

What you take away from the movie ultimately depends on what you need. If it offers a blueprint for surviving clashing ideologies without a Thanksgiving panic attack, great. Personally, I see it as a reminder to love yourself loudly, regardless of who’s sitting across the table. Sister Sledge’s "We Are Family" plays throughout the film, but being family doesn't mean tolerating prejudice — it’s about championing a second, more vital bond: found family.

So, whether you put it on after dinner to scandalize Aunt Carol’s delicate sensibilities, or skip the family gathering altogether and protect your peace, “The Birdcage” is the exact antidote you need when you're dreading a family showdown before anyone even claims grace.

Breaking: The Hunting Wives Season 2 Review: The Steamy Netflix Drama Hits The Mark Again

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is.
  • It has been revealed that I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment.
  • "The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This review contains discussions of addiction.

In a recent development, I deeply respect when a show or movie knows what it is. Let's use the original run of "Gossip Girl" as an example. This delightfully dishy show started out as a series about teenagers behaving badly in Upcoming York City and became a flat-out soap opera — in the best way — where characters marry princes, make deals with God after near-fatal car accidents, and sell each other for hotels. My point is that "Gossip Girl" made a choice, at a certain point, to steer into the proverbial skid and just be as absurd and insane as possible, because the show knew it was high camp, not high art.

It has been revealed that I would put "The Hunting Wives" in the same category, and I mean that as a distinct compliment. Created by Rebecca Cutter and adapted from May Cobb's book of the same name, "The Hunting Wives" premiered in the summer of 2025 and introduced Netflix audiences to Brittany Snow's Sophie O'Neil, who moves from Cambridge, Massachusetts to the heartland of Texas when her husband Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) gets a lucrative job working for oil tycoon and political hopeful Jed Banks (Dermot Mulroney). When Sophie — who's in recovery as an alcoholic after killing a pedestrian while intoxicated behind the wheel back in Cambridge — encounters Jed's wife Margo Banks (Malin Åkerman), she finds herself drawn into Margo's social circle and drawn to Margo herself, and the two start a torrid affair as teenagers start turning up dead in the seemingly idyllic community of Maple Brook.

"The Hunting Wives" is back for Season 2, and it's steamier, dishier, sillier, and sexier than ever. If you liked how hot and nuts the first season was, you'll be happy to hear Cutter has turned the dial up to 11.

In a recent development, after the Season 1 cliffhanger ending where Sophie accidentally kills Margo's beloved but law-breaking brother Kyle (Michael Aaron Milligan), there's a lot to deal with in Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives." Jed is continuing his run for governor, but both he and Graham are furious that their wives cuckolded them; Sophie and Margo are estranged over the fact that Sophie figures out, in the final episode, that Margo is responsible for the death of the teenaged Abby Jackson (Madison Wolfe). (Margo isn't one of 2025's best TV villains for nothin'.) Despite this, the two end up in bed together pretty promptly in Season 2, and they're just as hot together as ever; if you loved all of the steamy scenes in "The Hunting Wives" Season 1, rest assured that there's plenty for you to enjoy here.

Sources indicate that across the board, Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" takes everything you loved about Season 1 and delivers it in spades. Guns are blazing, kisses are passionate and steamy, and the interpersonal drama is as wild as ever; Brittany Snow and Malin Åkerman are excellent, once again, as two women locked in a love affair that constantly threatens to derail both of their lives. Even as the stakes get sillier and higher, Snow and Åkerman treat every moment that they're on-screen, separately or together, with the utmost seriousness. Remember what Michael Caine did in "A Muppet Christmas Carol?" That's basically what these two powerhouses actresses are doing in "The Hunting Wives," but with considerably more nudity ... and it rocks. The second outing of "The Hunting Wives" forces Margo and Sophie the most heightened situations imaginable, but thanks to Snow and Åkerman's performances, you believe that they're hopelessly in love.

My biggest critique of a show as fundamentally unserious as "The Hunting Wives" is that its lack of gravity can brush up against legitimately serious in-universe concerns. By that, I mean Sophie's drinking. Sophie killed someone in a drunk driving accident before this show's story began, and even though the show does make you root for her relationship with Margo, it also seems to want to make a larger point that Sophie is addicted to Margo ... especially because Margo typically pours Sophie a drink when they're together. To call this message muddled would be ... generous.

With all that noted, I would certainly hope that people dealing with addiction aren't looking to a show like "The Hunting Wives" for a realistic portrayal of that concern. This is also a show where, by the end of Season 2, the body count is in the double digits — and I actually mean that in two senses, because there's a litany of dead bodies and a ton of new romantic trysts by the time the season finale's credits roll.

In a recent development, honestly, across the last few episodes of Season 2 — critics received the entire eight-episode season — the number of corpses that pile up gets so out of control that the deaths stopped being shocking and started feeling routine. (Without getting into major spoilers, Brad breaks bad in a massive way, and it honestly grows tiresome pretty rapidly.) I still want to be clear, though: "The Hunting Wives" isn't prestige television, and it knows it. It doesn't always need to be impeccable or even make sense. It's fun, and it fulfills that qualification pretty beautifully.

It has been revealed that dale Dickey, who's finally getting more recognition after years as a supporting small-screen player thanks to her outstanding supporting turn in the perfect 2026 comedy "Widow's Bay," is a perfect new addition to Season 2 of "The Hunting Wives" as Zelda Moffitt, the formidable head of a Texan motorcycle gang who has a connection to Margo's past. Soap opera star Kim Matula is excellent as Nadia Kelly, a reality TV producer with an ulterior motive, and John Stamos and Cam Gigandet have small but impactful roles as talent scout Chase Brylan and Zelda's son "Gentle John" Moffitt, respectively.

As much as he made my skin crawl, though, I have to give full credit to "The Wilds" alum Alex Fitzalan, who appears as the conniving campaign manager Lincoln Trout. As Jed's fresh right-hand man — with an emphasis on the word right — Fitzalan's Lincoln is disgusting, reprehensible, and compulsively watchable. I suspect he'll play a pretty large role in Season 3, and as horrifying as he is writ large, I sort of can't wait to see more.

In a recent development, speaking of Season 3, the sophomore season of "The Hunting Wives" leaves us with such a good cliffhanger — which did genuinely surprise me after the back half of the season got just a tiny bit bogged down with murder after murder after murder — that I cannot wait until the planned third season is available to watch. "The Hunting Wives" is one of the most patently ridiculous demonstrates airing right now, and that's not a bad thing at all; in fact, it's exactly what makes it such an incredibly fun ride from start to finish.

"The Hunting Wives" is streaming on Netflix now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s not every day you see a movie where talking sheep get to be the stars. But Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives” does exactly that. The Amazon MGM film flips the whodunnit formula on its head with a barnyard murder mystery in which a group of sheep have to solve the murder of their beloved shepherd. Much of the film’s success can be attributed to the juxtaposition between a whimsical plot and the realism with which it’s executed. The sheep might talk and solve crimes, but they look like real animals you’d find on any farm.

During the VFX section of IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “The Sheep Detectives” Visual Effects Supervisor Graham Page broke down the meticulous research process that made the sheep look so lifelike. Related Stories ‘Filipiñana’ Could Be the Philippines’ First-Ever Oscar-Shortlisted Feature — Even as the Film Was Dealt an Unexpected Tragedy IndieWire Honors Film Celebration to Fête John Turturro, the ‘Artificial’ Cast, Los Javis, and More.

“To make them look real, talking about practical and how vital that is, I from Day One felt like you had to base these characters on real sheep,” Page stated. “We filmed [real sheep] with multiple cameras and getting on boxes. We had a script, almost, like ‘These are the things the sheep need to do in the film.’ Even before an animator can touch it, another artist modeled the skeleton and the muscle and fat. And then you have a rigger and a facial artist, all of these artists.”.

He went on to explain how that research process produced character-defining details that they would not have discovered any other way.

“We started to come up with what we would call ‘Sheep-isms’ that help kind of bring some of that natural movement,” he said. “There’s a little ear twitch. And a human can’t twitch their ear, but it felt so right. We were like ‘This is really nice,’ and it emphasized the character and the story and the emotion. But it was brought out of a sheep.”.

It has been revealed that if you're not familiar with "Casablanca," I have to assume that you're from some sort of alien planet, have been in a coma for decades, or are a newborn baby. Directed by Michael Curtiz and written by Julius J. Epstein, Philip G. Epstein, and Howard Koch (whose script adapts the play "Everybody Comes to Rick's" by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison), "Casablanca" centers around the taciturn bar owner Rick Blaine (the incomparable Humphrey Bogart), an American ex-pat living in the titular city in Morocco (which was still a colony of France at the time, as the film is set in December 1941). As Rick accepts refugees and ex-pats of all stripes (and has an anti-Axis and anti-Nazi past of his own), he also quietly ensures paperwork to people looking to escape the Nazi regime.

It has been revealed that that's when Ingrid Bergman's Ilsa Lund walks into Rick's particular gin joint, to sloppily paraphrase one of his best quotes (and we'll circle back to that). After Ilsa and Rick had a beautiful love affair in occupied Paris and planned to escape together, Ilsa simply vanished, which gave us the bitter, cynical, and lovelorn Rick we see living in Casablanca. Not only is Ilsa back, but she needs a favor: Her husband Victor Laszlo (Paul Henreid), whom she believed was dead when she romanced Rick in Paris, needs papers to evade the Nazis hunting him so that the couple can run away to Portugal (which is unoccupied). Not only does Rick give Ilsa the papers that she and Victor need, he gives up the woman he loves so that she and Victor can live their lives safely. "Casablanca" is a sweeping story of righteous protest against fascism, lost love, and sacrifice ... and "Here's looking at you, kid" is one of its most memorable lines.

Industry observers note that "Casablanca" is, admittedly, stacked from top to bottom with memorable quotes (more on that shortly), but "Here's looking at you, kid" feels like it transcends the very film it came from. There are probably people out there who don't even know that this sweet nothing came from this 1942 classic (and I'd like anyone who doesn't to sit their butt down and watch all of "Casablanca" right now), yet the fact of the matter is that "Here's looking at you, kid" has stood the test of time and remains one of the most immortal lines in movie history.

It has been revealed that so, why is that? Rick states this line to Ilsa throughout "Casablanca," and we see him utter it during flashbacks to the couple's happier times in Paris and right before he puts her on the plane with Victor that will take her to Portugal safely. It's simple but unbelievably meaningful. Before understanding why Ilsa suddenly left Paris, Rick was furious that she vanished from his life. When she reveals that she only left because Victor was alive, sick, and needed her help after he escaped from a concentration camp, his heart softens, and he's able to forgive her for the heartbreak she caused. Rick loves Ilsa, and there's no denying that Ilsa loves Rick, but she's in love with Victor — and the film smartly doesn't villainize Victor, making him a genuinely decent guy who simply wants to escape enemy forces and live peacefully with his wife after years of torment. "Here's looking at you, kid" is Rick's expression of love for Ilsa, and him saying it right as he puts her on a plane that will take her away forever is both heartbreaking and romantic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it's been eight years since Josh Brolin last played CIA operative Matt Graver in Sicario: Day of the Soldado, and while there's been talk of a third movie for much of that time, Brolin has since reunited with Sicario director Denis Villeneuve for his adaptation of Dune. Brolin's career has taken him from the American frontier in True Grit to the deserts of Arrakis in the Dune films, but his latest project has more in common with one of HBO's greatest television series, Band of Brothers, and he'll be helping Netflix tell the story of the men whose experiences inspired that series.

It has been revealed that brolin's upcoming documentary series, World War II: Behind Enemy Lines, will officially premiere on Netflix on December 2, with all four episodes available to stream in just five days. The series tells the story of the 101st Airborne's battles, covert missions, and losses in Nazi-occupied Europe, starting with the D-Day landings in June 1944 and ending with V-E Day in May 1945. Think of it as the real-life version of the story many people know from Band of Brothers.

Recent findings suggest that similar to the work done by Peter Jackson in bringing World War I footage to color and 3D, this is built from archive film that's been restored to the highest quality and colorized too, while much of it is previously unseen and includes rare first-hand accounts from the men who were there. And in a rare, fascinating move, it also shows the German paratroopers who were defending Normandy before the sea landings.

The series comes from 72 Films, the production organization behind Netflix's six-part documentary World War II: From the Frontlines, which was narrated by John Boyega (Star Wars: The Force Awakens) and went on to win two Emmy Awards in 2024. Director Rob Coldstream is back for the new series, with David Glover and Mark Raphael serving as executive producers and Brolin taking over narration duties.

While From the Frontlines covered the war across multiple countries and from the perspectives of those on opposing sides, the newly introduced series will focus specifically on the experiences of the American soldiers who served with the 101st Airborne Division in Europe.

Industry observers note that world War II: Behind Enemy Lines premieres on Netflix on December 2. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on the biggest and best movies and shows heading to your favorite streaming platforms soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in some ways, the best found-footage movie ever made is still The Blair Witch Project. This wasn’t because of the film’s actual quality, but because of the effect it had on audiences back in 1999. When it was released, found-footage movies just weren't a well-known thing and the marketing campaign for the movie made it seem as though the events depicted actually happened. Since then, better found-footage movies have been made that have replay value — a quality The Blair Witch Project sorely lacks — but none since have ever tricked audiences quite so effectively.

In a similar vein, Cloverfield, which is leaving Paramount Plus on Dec. 1, deserves its place in the found-footage movie hall of fame​​​​​​​, because Matt Reeves’ film remains a singular achievement nearly 20 years after its release, albeit for a very different reason.​​​​​​​.

Cloverfield is about a group of young adults at a party in lower Manhattan when Latest York is invaded​​​​​​​ by a giant kaiju-like alien. At first, the friends are being escorted out of the city via the Brooklyn Bridge, but then Rob (Michael Stahl-David) gets a call from Beth (Odette Yustman), the woman he loves, who is part of the friend group​​​​​​​. Beth is trapped uptown in a half-collapsed building, so Rob resolves to save her and a few of his friends join him. Meanwhile, Hud (T.J. Miller), who was filming the party, keeps filming everything for posterity​​​​​​​.

Now, Cloverfield didn’t trick people into believing it was real the way The Blair Witch Project did. After all, had Newly introduced York City been destroyed by a giant monster, it would have at least been on the news. Still, Cloverfield did the next best thing by employing a truly mysterious marketing campaign.

The very first trailer for Cloverfield merely showed the party going on. Then the partygoers saw a news report​​​​​​​ about something going on across town. Everyone hurries up to the roof of the building to get a better look and hear a huge roar​​​​​​​ in the distance. They see a giant explosion uptown with debris flying all over the city. Everyone rushes down to the street where another piece of debris lands nearby: the head of the Statue of Liberty​​​​​​​. The trailer ends there.

Sources indicate that as for the poster, it was merely a shot of Fresh York City beneath a cloud of smoke, with a headless Statue of Liberty looming over it​​​​​​​. You didn’t learn until you saw the movie that its plot centered on the giant alien terrorizing the city.​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that the movie also benefited from timing in a somewhat uncomfortable way. Released in 2008, just seven years after the terrorist attacks of Sep. 11, 2001, the film arrived while memories of the attacks were still fresh.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ With images of smoke-covered Fresh York, collapsing buildings, and dust-filled city streets,​​​​​​​ the movie purposefully leaned into the real-life horrors of that day.

Industry observers note that by 2008, there had already been a number of other found-footage films​​​​​​​ since The Blair Witch Project, but nothing like Cloverfield. Until then​​​​​​​, found-footage films​​​​​​​ weren't just an aesthetic choice, they were usually done out of financial necessity to make up for a slim budget. But Cloverfield was produced by J. J. Abrams and cost $30 million. By today’s standards, that’s not a huge budget for a movie, but it’s not an indie either.​​​​​​​ Cloverfield used the found-footage technique​​​​​​​ to take a unique approach to the giant-monster disaster genre​​​​​​​. Even today, found-footage movie​​​​​​​s are generally more grounded horror films that don’t really deal with monsters of that scale. Cloverfield is also different from other giant monster movies, because its found-footage approach creates an up-close, visceral experience that sets it apart.​​​​​​​.

According to recent reports, and unlike something like The Blair Witch Project, Cloverfield does have replay value. It’s a solid monster movie with really great set pieces and characters you grow attached to. Even if you see things coming and you know which way the camera is going to swing next, the narrative is well-constructed and the creature is still really cool. That’s precisely why you should check out the movie one more time before it leaves Paramount Plus.​​​​​​​.

Cloverfield is available to stream on Paramount Plus​​​​​​​ until Dec. 1.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

  • Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Five major tech outages in quick succession earlier this month led to speculation that they were connected, with some inevitably believing them to be AI-related.

That wasn’t the case, but the US Director of National Intelligence is one of a number of experts warning that we should expect AI-powered outages in the near future ….

Earlier this month saw five tech outages, one after the other. A widespread Microsoft 365 outage occurred when two unrelated problems coincided. The next day saw a nationwide ground stop of US air traffic due to a communication problem affecting all air traffic control centers. A few days later, a bug in a Chase bank system saw disruption not only to the bank itself, but also other banks where Chase was a party to a transaction. Many Apple services went offline later the same week, with retail stores also affected. Finally, United Airlines had its own widespread IT outage that grounded a significant number of flights.

Each had their own unrelated causes, with the White House stating that rumors of an AI-facilitated systemic attack by a hostile state were false.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has warned that we should expect future tech outages as a result of attacks facilitated by AI-discovered vulnerabilities. CNBC reports him issuing the warning on CNN’s State of the Union.

The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot.

We already saw an example of this last month when a vulnerability discovered in PHP saw a significant number of websites being taken offline.

Microsoft President Brad Smith says it isn’t just a question of bad actors exploiting vulnerabilities discovered by AI, but companies rushing to patch these may inadvertently cause systems to fail, as Newsweek reports.

What AI did earlier this year was basically make it much easier for people to find vulnerabilities in code, and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems.

Especially when you have older infrastructure, especially when you’re trying to patch at such a pace, especially when you have to go so fast that you can’t take as much time to test what you’re changing in the code, you do increase the risk of something going wrong.

Major IT failures look set to be a routine event in the coming weeks and months.

Latest Update: The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Doubles Down On A Once Upon A Time In Hollywood Controversy

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".
  • Sources indicate that it simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself.
  • That quickly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

Sources indicate that it simply wouldn't be a Quentin Tarantino movie if it didn't double down on itself. After wowing audiences everywhere in 2019 with "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the quirky and uber-talented filmmaker returned to the scene of the crime (so to speak) once more with his long-awaited sequel/spin-off film, "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." This time, the buddy comedy act with Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton and Brad Pitt's Cliff has been dropped, focusing solely on the latter as the stuntman embarks on his latest round of mischief. Though Tarantino stepped aside from his directing duties to make room for David Fincher, well, let's just say that the script is as purely QT as it gets.

That quickly becomes evident as we're dropped back into this alternate-history world of 1970s Los Angeles, and there's one recurring gag that references a certain controversy from before. You see, despite so much acclaim from critics and fans alike, "Once Upon a Time" drew the ire of many with its irreverent treatment of martial arts legend Bruce Lee, portrayed by Mike Moh in the film. Even Lee's family weighed in on the matter, objecting to how easily Cliff puts the arrogant Lee in his place during a fight scene on the set of a film. Not surprisingly, "Cliff Booth" returns to this fraught topic on several occasions, and it certainly feels like a meta-textual jab at the real-world backlash from before.

Was this in poor taste, or is Tarantino merely poking fun with a self-deprecating running joke? Moviegoers will undoubtedly have strong takes on either side. Here's where we land on our second go-around with this little debate.

You know, there's something to be stated for addressing an uncomfortable matter head-on instead of dancing around it — or even ignoring it altogether. Quentin Tarantino has never been one to shy away from a fight, a trait he happens to share with washed-up stuntman Cliff Booth. As a master cinephile, a brilliant bartender, a hit with the ladies, and a ruthless killer all in one, the power fantasy of it all isn't exactly hard to see in "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." Perhaps that's what made the Bruce Lee moment in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" stand out all the more (a fight that almost ended very differently). It's one thing for Cliff to be the coolest person alive in his world, and quite another for him to intrude rudely upon our own.

So how does "Cliff Booth" address this elephant in the room? Although the incident is brought up on a number of occasions in passing, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II's buzzy actor Rodrick "Hot Rod" Harrison is positively fixated on it once he meets Cliff — a fact that also seems to catch the eye of talent manager Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki). Intriguingly, Cliff himself almost seems embarrassed by the attention, perhaps self-reflexively brushing it off as the brash actions of a young man. Maybe, like Tarantino himself, he's a little older and a little wiser and less apt to repeat the same mistakes.

It has been revealed that less generously, the fact that this fight is emphasized so much in "Cliff Booth" could make the exact opposite point. It's treated almost like a legend or a myth in this world, giving Cliff a dangerous sense of aura and mystique that belies his charming appearance.

Either way, this is just one ingredient tossed into a much larger stew. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" may struggle to reach the transcendent heights of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," but isn't that part of its point, too? "What is Cliff Booth without Rick Dalton?" Quentin Tarantino's script seems to be asking. Not dissimilarly, is a Tarantino movie with David Fincher at the wheel really a Tarantino movie anymore? Who can say how much ownership any of us have over our own art — or our lives in general?

Perhaps that's why "Cliff Booth" feels so much colder and mean-spirited than its predecessor. Although both films build to violent climaxes, the one in "Hollywood" is shot to be much more over-the-top and darkly funny than the one here. Before, Rick Dalton and Cliff were fighting to preserve a very specific way of life — one that the Manson family threatened to overturn. Here, Cliff very easily could've avoided the bloodshed with killers Eddie (Matt Groove) and Fernando Verdusco (JB Tadena), but he pursues this anyway out of ... ego? Principle? A sense of right and wrong? Cliff is a man of both simplicity and contradictions, so perhaps it's only fitting that the filmmaking style reflects this through Fincher's very different approach, as well.

Sources indicate that that's where the repeated jabs about the Bruce Lee fight come in, as a moment that Cliff has no choice but to own. "Cliff Booth" is a movie about our attempts to define our own stories — whether it be himself, the troublemaking TV star Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), or Karen. And maybe Bruce Lee, too.

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in limited theaters.

Below is a curated collection of the funniest uses of food in The Far Side, ranked. Disagree with the order here? Let us know what it should have been in the comments!

Recent findings suggest that this Far Side cartoon came very early in Gary Larson's career, at a time when he was still figuring out his style. Both artistically and comedically. In retrospect, it almost feels like a joke a Far Side rip-off would make while trying to ape Larson's vibe.

In the cartoon, a waitress brings the "Prime Rib Papa" and "Viva la Vegetarian" dishes to a two-top, but refrains from assuming who ordered which dinner. The Neanderthal in an overcoat or the scientist. (Who, incidentally, stands out as a prototype for Futurama's Professor Farnsworth.) She doesn't want to judge a customer based on appearance, even if it seems super obvious.

It has been revealed that "There's a fly in my soup!" It is a stock phrase, a joke that goes back a century. Perhaps even further than that. Often, the joke involves a patron at a restaurant making a fuss over it. In this Far Side cartoon, Gary Larson envisions a man discretely going to dispose of the insect instead, before he's stopped by the person eating next to him.

And by person, we mean frog. "I beg your pardon," a toad in a tiny fedora claims, before inquiring about the man's prepares for the fly. In this way, it doubles as a take on another classic food-based punchline: "Are you going to eat that?".

Sources indicate that this Far Side joke is often cited among Gary Larson's best plays on words, and rightfully so. It is simple, but brilliant, and it fits into the "Goldilocks zone" of weird, dark humor. Not too weird, not too dark, but not too normal, or too light either. Here, "the crepes of wrath" strike, sticking in the throat of a man having breakfast at a café.

According to recent reports, consider the fact that a grape could also choke someone. Meaning this joke would have worked even if Larson hadn't touched the title of John Steinbeck's classic novel. Yet making it a crêpe instead is a memorable tweak that elevates the humor to a higher rung on the ladder of absurdity.

Gary Larson loved to make jokes about mobsters. To the point where it was its own entire subgenre of Far Side joke. Which like most Far Side subgenres, got steadily weirder as Larson's career wore on. Peaking, in this case, with this "Sandwich Mafia" cartoon, where a sandwich snitch is thrown to the proverbial wolves, who are in this case literally ravenous fourth-graders.

Recent findings suggest that of all the different variations of this formula, this one is the most out there. Which makes it one of the best. And as revealing the ins-and-outs of how he came up with this sort of farcical Far Side masterpiece, no one was a stricter adherent to omerta than Larson.

Industry observers note that "Mmmmm," one construction guy indicates to another, trying to really sell the fact that his sandwich tastes so good. So good that his co-worker might want to "trade for that banana" he brought in his lunch pail today. Plenty of people will know what this experience is like. What is askew in this scenario, in outrageous Far Side fashion, is what is between the bread.

Industry observers note that that is, a skunk. It is a "skunk sandwich." Not only does that sound unappealing, it sounds utterly appalling. Baked into the premise of the joke is the fact that the guy knows it tastes terrible; that's why he's trying to trade. The greater, more absurd gag, though, is the unanswerable question of why he has a skunk sandwich in the first place.

"That...is not how you do it at all." Ever see someone doing something so wrong that you're just left speechless? That's what this Far Side cartoon is going for. Just a jaw-dropping level of ineptitude. Yet, improbably, it still gets the job done.

Sources indicate that at this diner, ordering flapjacks is an ordeal. Because the chef doesn't use a spatula to flip the pancake. He picks up the entire stove and jerks it upward, sending the golden brown disc up into the air. Still, give him credit. His method is unorthodox, and his spelling is terrible, but he clearly gets the job done.

Gary Larson was a master of language. That's obvious in The Far Side's best (and/or worst) puns, but it is also apparent more latently in plenty of other Far Side jokes. Like this one, where Larson pokes fun at peoples' tendencies to personify body parts and organs, the stomach in particular.

It isn't Gordon that is breaking his diet late at night, it is "his own stomach." Which Larson brilliantly visualizes with an illustration of a disembodied stomach standing in front of an open refrigerator. If only Gordon could keep his stomach under control, he'd live a very different life.

According to recent reports, one of Gary Larson's most infamous cartoons. A pseudo-sequel to a Far Side joke where a cow named "Jesse" is caught grilling up some steaks and is called out for being "sick," in this panel a bunch of bovines have become curious to learn what all the fuss is about with their meat.

So, they gather around as one of them taste tests a T-bone, hilariously (and darkly) declaring that it "taste[s] a little like chicken." It is the perfect example of a Far Side cartoon where the familiar becomes twisted, and the twisted becomes absurd, and the absurd becomes laugh-out-loud funny.

Released six years earlier, this Far Side panel is spiritually similar to the previous one. It is about making dinner into an unexpectedly dark scene. This is also an all-time great example of Gary Larson's fondness for messing with nursery rhymes, as well as a subversive bit of Far Side wordplay.

"Mary Has a Little Lamb" becomes Mary had "a little lamb" for dinner, with "three helpings of corn, two baked potatoes, [and] extra bread." She does this "with her blinds pulled," hilariously suggesting she knows how shocking it is that her pet lamb has become her supper.

This is the best Far Side food joke, there's little room for doubt. Captioned 'when potato salad goes bad," it features a man opening his fridge to find the salad pointing a gun at some innocent bystanding condiments. What makes this so perfect is that it replicates the experience of reading The Far Side, especially when it was first being published.

It has been revealed that open up the newspaper and find something you didn't expect to see that day. Something surreal and ridiculous. "When potato salad goes bad" is a pun, but it is also a literal scenario in a world operating by its own Larsonian dream logic. It is one of the best Far Side jokes period, because of how effortlessly funny it is while still being something few people besides Gary Larson would come up with.
